canonical.summary: Lesions first develop on lower leaves as small brownish-black spots that expand to 1/4-1/2 inch with characteristic concentric rings producing a 'bull's eye' or 'target-spot' appearance; surrounding tissue may yellow and entire leaves may become chlorotic, with dark sunken fruit lesions also showing concentric rings.
diagnostic_features: Characteristic concentric rings in the darkened lesion area giving a 'bull's eye' or 'target-spot' appearance on lower leaves; on fruit, lesions are sunken, leathery, dark brown to black with concentric rings, often entering through the calyx around the stem attachment; potato tuber lesions are dark, sunken, circular, often bordered by purple to gray raised tissue with dry, leathery, brown underlying flesh.
treatments: Maintain plant vigor through adequate fertilization to reduce host susceptibility
Remove volunteer weeds and volunteer tomatoes that serve as an inoculum source
Rotate every 2-3 years away from tomato to reduce inoculum density

Use resistant or tolerant cultivars (e.g., 'Mountain Magic', 'Mountain Fresh Plus F1', 'Bush Celebrity Hybrid', 'Big Beef Hybrid', 'Celebrity Hybrid', 'Rutgers', 'Juliet F1', 'Tommy Toe', 'Old Brooks', 'Cabernet F1')
Start with disease-free seed, transplants, and seed tubers
Control susceptible weeds (e.g., horsenettle) and eliminate cull piles
Plow under plant debris after harvest
Time irrigation to avoid late afternoon or evening; use proper plant spacing to reduce leaf wetness duration
Stake or trellis plants to improve air circulation and reduce soil contact; use mulch to prevent spore splash
Avoid working plants when they are wet; prune the bottom-most leaves as the plant grows

Apply fungicides preventatively (7-14 day intervals) — e.g., azoxystrobin + chlorothalonil (Quadris Opti), azoxystrobin + difenoconazole (Quadris Top), boscalid (Endura), chlorothalonil (Bravo), cyprodinil + fludioxinil (Switch), difenoconazole + benzovindiflupyr (Aprovia Top), difenoconazole + cyprodinil (Inspire Super), fenamidone (Reason), flutriafol (Rhyme), fluopyram + trifloxystrobin (Luna Sensation), fluopyram + pyrimethanil (Luna Tranquility), fluxaypyroxad + pyraclostrobin (Priaxor), mandipropamid + difenoconazole (Revus Top), penthiopyrad (Fontelis), pydiflumetofen + fludioxonil (Miravis Prime), pyrimethanil (Scala), strobilurin products (Quadris, Cabrio, Gem, Evito)
Schedule spray applications using spore trapping or forecasting systems (TOM-CAST)

Organic options: Bacillus amyloliquefaciens strain D747 (Double Nickel 55), Bacillus mycoides isolate J (LifeGard WG), Bacillus pumilus strain QST 2808 (Sonata), Bacillus subtilis strain IAB/BS03 (AVIV), Bacillus subtilis strain QST 713 (Cease, Serenade ASO, Serenade Opti), extract of Reynoutria sachalinensis (Regalia), fixed copper, polyoxin D zinc salt (OSO 5%SC), potassium bicarbonate (Carb-O-Nator), Streptomyces lydicus WYEC 108 (Actinovate AG)

treatments.quote: Maintain plant vigor. Maintaining adequate fertilization and improving host vigor can reduce susceptibility to early blight. Remove volunteer weeds. Apply fungicides preventatively. Plant tolerant varieties.

canonical.summary: A brown-to-black lesion develops on the lower stem at the soil line and can girdle the stem, causing sudden permanent wilt of above-ground parts; under moist conditions a white mycelial mat (often fan-shaped) appears at the stem base, followed by tan to reddish-brown spherical sclerotia (1-2 mm); fruit in contact with soil develop sunken, water-soaked, star-shaped lesions that collapse within 3-4 days.
diagnostic_features: White mycelial mat with a distinct fan-shaped pattern plus tan to reddish-brown spherical sclerotia (1-2 mm / 0.04-0.08 inch) at the stem base near the soil line; fruit lesions are sunken, water-soaked, soft, and star-shaped with no offensive odor, distinguishing it from other soilborne wilt diseases.
treatments: Avoid planting in fields with a history of southern blight
Crop rotation with non-host plants such as corn, wheat, barley, and other small grains/grasses; wait 5-6 years before returning with the same crop family
Deep plowing (>4-8 inches) to bury infected plant debris and sclerotia (pathogen is highly aerobic)
Ensure the previous crop residue is fully decomposed prior to planting
Sanitation: early detection and removal of symptomatic plants, crop residues, and weeds; use protective gloves, boots, and disinfectants
Use certified, pathogen-free seed and transplants
Modify planting dates to avoid wet/warm conditions favorable to disease (77-95°F)
Wider plant spacing to improve airflow
Maintain or raise soil pH by liming (lower pH encourages disease)
Avoid injuring plants during cultivation
Use physical barriers (aluminum foil or plastic bags around the stem at the soil line for home gardeners; plastic mulch in commercial fields/tunnels)
Apply straw mulch to the soil
Use grafted tomato rootstocks tolerant to southern blight ('Maxifort', 'Big Power', 'Beaufort')
Use ammonium-source nitrogen instead of nitrate
Soil solarization (raise soil temperatures to 50-55°C / 122-131°F for up to 6 hours)
Anaerobic soil disinfestation
Biological control: Trichoderma harzianum, Trichoderma viride, certain mycorrhizal fungi, Penicillium spp., Gliocladium virens, Bacillus subtilis (often combined with soil solarization)
Soil fumigants: chloropicrin, metam-sodium (sodium metam), allyl isothiocyanate
Pre-plant fungicide: pentachloronitrobenzene (PCNB / Terraclor) applied as a transplant solution or in-furrow soil spray; flutolanil
Strobilurin fungicides: pyraclostrobin (Cabrio EG), azoxystrobin, fluoxastrobin (Aftershock, Evito 480 SC)
SDHI fungicides: fluxapyroxad + pyraclostrobin (Priaxor 500 SC), penthiopyrad (Fontelis)
Triazole fungicides: tebuconazole, prothioconazole
Difenoconazole + benzovindiflupyr (Aprovia Top)

canonical.summary: Leaf lesions are small, irregular to circular, gray with reddish-brown borders, occurring most commonly on the upper leaf surface; lesions start as dark, water-soaked spots (generally 1-5 mm) and as they age the central area becomes gray to light brown with dark, red-brown margins; in severe cases the disease causes premature leaf drop and spreads to stems and pods.
diagnostic_features: Reddish-purple margins surround the gray centers on mature lesions; on some varieties, lesions may have light green to yellow halos; fuzzy, gray sporulation (conidia) can occur in lesions on the leaf underside; small black dots that resemble fine ground pepper (fungal spores) may be visible in the middle of lesions. Stem lesions are elongated gray with purple margins; pod lesions are circular, gray with purple margins.
treatments: Plant resistant soybean varieties (varieties with resistance to all known races are available)
Rotate to non-host crops (e.g., corn, sorghum, wheat, alfalfa, small grains) to reduce survival of C. sojina
Tillage / deep tillage to encourage breakdown of crop debris and reduce fungal overwintering
Plant certified, disease-free seed to reduce seedborne infections
Apply foliar fungicides between R3 and R5 growth stages (late flowering to pod filling)
Avoid strobilurin (QoI) fungicides as solo applications due to widespread fungicide resistance
Rotate fungicide chemistries or use products with multiple modes of action when spraying multiple times per season

profiles.disease: Bacterial Canker And Wilt Of Tomato

canonical.summary: Symptoms include small white raised spots and yellow-to-tan interveinal patches on leaves with brown burned-looking margins, one-sided wilting of lower leaves, brown streaks in the vascular system with stem cankers that may exude yellow sticky fluid, and 'bird's eye' spots (small ~1/4 inch raised white spots with tan/brown centers and cream-colored halos) on fruit.
diagnostic_features: Bird's eye spot on fruit (small ~1/4 inch raised white spots with tan/brown centers surrounded by a light yellow or cream-colored halo); brown streaks in the vascular system visible when stem is cut, with mealy pith; yellow sticky fluid exuding from squeezed cut stem; one-sided wilting of lower leaves; marginal leaf browning that looks burned on the edges; dark sunken leaf veins on young greenhouse plants.
treatments: Remove leaves with symptoms
Crop rotation to a non-host crop for 3-4 years (no tomato, potato, pepper, or eggplant); UMN also notes a shorter 2-3 year option
Plant certified pathogen-free seed from a reputable supplier; do not save seeds from infected plants
Treat saved seed before planting: soak in 1 part germicidal bleach to 4 parts water for 1 minute, then rinse in water for 5 minutes
Hot water seed treatment: soak seeds in 122°F water for 25 minutes
Seed may also be treated with dilute solutions of sodium hypochlorite
Purchase healthy transplants from a reputable grower; inspect and avoid transplants with spots, discoloration, or that have been pruned or cut back
Keep tomato leaves as dry as possible — water with drip irrigation or a soaker hose, in the morning so leaves dry quickly
Use filtered and/or treated irrigation water
Space plants so that air flows between them
Stake or cage plants, and clean and sanitize stakes/cages each year
Dispose of wooden stakes from an infested field; discard strings and wooden stakes
Disinfect tools and equipment between seasons with a commercial greenhouse sanitizer or a 1:9 bleach:water solution for 1-5 minutes
Regularly clean pruning tools; alternate between two pruners between plants to allow proper soaking time
Wash re-used pots and trays to remove crop debris, then sanitize; use new potting media stored in a sanitary environment
Wash hands, exposed clothing, and boots regularly; designate specific boots and clothes for each greenhouse or bay; wash hands before and after moving between greenhouses
Eliminate or reduce weeds (especially Solanaceae such as nightshades) and volunteer tomato/pepper plants during rotation
Avoid working in fields when the foliage is wet with rain, irrigation, or dew
Immediately remove and destroy all diseased material; in greenhouse/high tunnel production, bag and remove infected plants including roots, plus adjacent plants even if they appear healthy
Remove symptomatic plants and adjacent plants during transplant production
Remove or plow in remaining plant debris immediately after harvest to encourage decomposition
Switch to hydroponic tomato production where the pathogen has built up in the soil and rotation is a challenge
Regular, preventative spraying of copper compounds provides some protection from bacterial canker
Sprays during transplant production are more effective in prevention than sprays post-transplanting or once symptoms appear in the field

canonical.summary: Plants wilt in the field, often recovering overnight but continuing to wilt each day; wilt progresses down the vine until the entire vine wilts or dies, with leaves yellowing and browning at the margins before completely withering.
diagnostic_features: Sever an infected vine close to the crown, press the cross-sections together briefly, then slowly pull them apart; thread-like sticky strands of bacterial ooze connecting the cut surfaces confirm the pathogen.
treatments: Manage cucumber beetles with appropriate insecticide programs (the most effective way to prevent bacterial wilt)
Rogue and bury (or otherwise remove) infected plants to prevent further spread and to keep beetles from moving the bacteria to other cucurbits
Use floating/spunbonded row covers as seedlings emerge; remove them when flowers appear to allow pollination
Use insect exclusion screens (e.g., 0.8 x 1.0 mm screen size) in hoop houses or greenhouses to keep beetles out while allowing ventilation
Plant a sprayed perimeter trap crop of Blue Hubbard squash to protect more susceptible crops
Remove or destroy crop residue to reduce overwintering sites for cucumber beetles
Use crop rotation to reduce beetle numbers in adjacent areas
Apply Surround (kaolin clay) to reduce beetle numbers
Plant cucurbit cultivars with resistance to bacterial wilt; resistant cucumber cultivars are being developed
Do not rely on copper sprays or bactericides: because the bacterium is transmitted systemically, copper sprays and direct bactericide applications are of no value

canonical.summary: Leaves develop large dark brown blotches with a green-gray edge (not confined by major leaf veins); irregularly shaped water-soaked lesions often with a lighter halo appear on younger leaves at the top of the canopy; stems show firm dark brown infections; tomato fruits develop firm, dark brown, greasy-to-leathery circular spots. In high humidity, thin powdery white fungal growth (sporangia) appears on infected tissue, especially the leaf underside.
diagnostic_features: Lesions occur on new growth at the top of the canopy (unlike early blight which starts on lower leaves), are light brown or tan (vs. dark brown with concentric rings for early blight); large dark brown leaf blotches have a green-gray edge that is not confined by major leaf veins; produces white cottony/powdery sporulation on the leaf underside under high humidity.
treatments: Plant tomatoes where no tomatoes, potatoes, peppers or eggplants have been for the past 3-4 years
Plant early in the season to escape high disease pressure later in the season
Keep leaves as dry as possible; water with drip irrigation or a soaker hose; water in the morning so leaves dry quickly
Stake or cage plants and space plants so that air flows between them
Remove or bury plants at the end of the season; manage cull piles so culls break down over winter
Scout plants often and remove infected plants, infected fruit, volunteers and weeds
Destroy potato cull piles before the growing season begins by burying, incorporating into fields, or feeding to livestock
Control volunteer potato plants, as infected plants can grow from infected tubers
Plant certified potato seed
Inspect tomato transplants for late blight symptoms prior to purchase and/or planting
If infection is found in only a few plants within a field, remove, disc-under, kill with herbicide or flame-kill infected plants to avoid spreading
Sign up to receive alerts at the USAblight website
Plant resistant varieties when possible (will still show some symptoms under highly favorable conditions)
Apply fungicides specific to water molds prior to infection when environmental conditions favor disease, repeated according to label instructions
Before disease occurs, apply fungicides at 7-10 day intervals; after disease is detected in your area, apply at 5-7 day intervals
Rotate fungicide groups and/or tank mix fungicides (e.g., with chlorothalonil) to avoid producing fungicide-resistant isolates

summary.quote: Leaves have large, dark brown blotches with a green gray edge; not confined by major leaf veins. Infections progress through leaflets and petioles, resulting in large sections of dry brown foliage. Stem infections are firm and dark brown with a rounded edge. In cool, wet weather, entire fields turn brown and wilted as if hit by frost. In tomatoes, firm, dark brown, circular spots grow to cover large parts of fruits. Spots may become mushy as secondary bacteria invade. In high humidity, thin powdery white fungal growth appears on infected leaves, tomato fruit and stems.

diagnostic_features.quote: Late blight can be differentiated from early blight on tomato and other foliar fungal diseases by where they occur on the plant. Lesions caused by late blight can be found anywhere on the plant, but are mostly found on the new growth whereas early blight typically starts on the lower leaves and slowly moves up the plant. Also, lesions caused by late blight tend to be light brown or tan in color while lesions caused by early blight tend to be dark brown in color with concentric rings.

canonical.summary: Small black spots (⅛ to ¼ inch) on leaves, often more prominent on the undersides, sometimes developing a yellow halo; on fruit, very small pinpoint-like spots ranging from brown to black, which may be raised, flat or sunken, with darker green haloes on green fruit and subtle yellow haloes on ripe fruit.
diagnostic_features: Small, angular (straight-edged) spots with yellow haloes on leaves; pinpoint-like superficial spots on fruit that do not penetrate deeply into the tissue.
treatments: Start by using high quality, pathogen-free seed or transplants from a reputable seed supplier or garden center
Consider treating the seed in hot water prior to planting to eliminate the pathogen
DO NOT use a sprinkler to water; instead use a soaker or drip hose to water at the bases of plants
Only work with tomato plants when they are dry

canonical.summary: Foliage suddenly turns an intense bright yellow at or near fruit set, beginning with interveinal yellowing and progressing to whole-vine yellowing; terminal leaves stand erect with curled margins, older leaves develop scorched margins, and plants ultimately wilt and collapse. Vascular tissue (phloem) at the crown turns a characteristic honey-brown rather than translucent green.
diagnostic_features: Honey-brown discoloration of the phloem in the crown and lower stem (visible at stem cross-section) is the key diagnostic; symptoms appear suddenly approximately 2 weeks before fruit maturity; terminal leaves stand erect, fail to expand, with margins curling inwards; unlike bacterial wilt, cut stems do NOT exude sticky ooze; in watermelon, fruit turn yellow as leaves discolor.
treatments: Control the squash bug (Anasa tristis) vector beginning at crop emergence or transplanting - this is the foundation of CYVD management
Target early-season adult squash bugs as they colonize the field; insecticide applications should hit young seedlings (< 3-5 true leaves) as soon as squash bugs are present
Manage the first generation of squash bugs during the nymphal stage to reduce the adult population; foliar sprays targeting newly hatched nymphs are more effective than against later stages
Repeat foliar sprays for extended periods of control
New generation synthetic pyrethroids (e.g., Capture, Brigade) tend to work better than most other materials against squash bug; Thionex may also be effective on squash bug and cucumber beetle
Systemic insecticides used for cucumber beetle management will provide up to 3 weeks of squash bug suppression
Crop rotation with non-cucurbit plants, or at a sufficient distance from previous cucurbit plantings
Remove crop debris and old/unharvested fruit to reduce overwintering squash bug populations

Use Hubbard squash (e.g., 'Blue Hubbard') as a perimeter/trap crop around later-planted pumpkins or other cucurbits; alternatively use early-planted straightneck summer squash ('Lemon Drop', 'Hyrific') as a border trap crop
Time the trap-crop spray just prior to main-crop emergence, with a second application at the first true-leaf stage of the main crop if needed
If infection has occurred, harvest and market fruit from infected pumpkins, winter squash, cantaloupe, or muskmelon vines early to avoid crop loss

canonical.summary: Infected plants in small clusters show foliar interveinal chlorosis followed by necrosis (foliar yellowing and death), with root rot, premature plant death, and stems that break at the crown when pulled; roots remaining attached are embedded with black fungal stroma along the primary root.
diagnostic_features: Black fungal tissue (stroma) along the primary root (and less frequently on lateral roots), white cottony fungal growth (mycelia) within the pith when roots are split longitudinally, and reproductive stromata ("dead man's fingers") on infected soybean debris and at the plant base under humid conditions — white at the tip (sometimes pinkish when young) turning black at maturity.
treatments: Practice crop rotation — rotation to cotton, corn, grain sorghum, rice or sugarcane will likely reduce the incidence and severity of TRD
Till fields after harvest/before planting (reduced or conventional) to facilitate breakdown of soybean debris and reduce inoculum
Use resistant cultivars — some commercially available soybean cultivars have shown resistance in greenhouse and field experiments
Differences in soybean variety susceptibility to TRD have been observed
Follow good sanitation practices — avoid moving soil from infested to non-infested fields, and clean soil and crop debris from machinery, clothes, boots, tools
Certain fungicides applied in-furrow have been observed to be beneficial (no fungicides are currently labeled for management of taproot decline)

treatments: Pine needle rust is a minor stress on the tree and no management is required.

Chemical management to control rust diseases is notoriously difficult and is not recommended.
Provide good air circulation; do not crowd plants.

treatments: Removal of crop debris and weed hosts (including brassica-family weeds and volunteers) may reduce inoculum.
Start with disease-free seed; ask your seed supplier if the lot has been tested for downy mildew, or hot-water treat your seeds.
Scout seedlings in the greenhouse/seedbed and maintain low humidity; check each seedling before transplanting and remove any showing symptoms.
Practice crop rotation with non-brassica crops (a two-year rotation away from brassicas, and rotate out of crucifers for at least two years).
Improve air circulation, avoid overcrowding seedlings, and irrigate early in the day so leaves are wet only for a few hours.
In the field, lower leaf wetness and canopy humidity by increasing spacing, controlling weeds, planting in the direction of prevailing winds, and planting in areas with full sun.
Collect and burn or bury as much of the crop as possible when harvest is complete; remove or bury infected crop debris near new plantings.
Plant resistant or tolerant cultivars (limited resistant varieties of cabbage and Chinese cabbage are available).
If fungicides are needed, spray with systemic metalaxyl/mefenoxam, or protectant mancozeb, copper, or chlorothalonil.

On transplants apply first spray as soon as seedlings appear and repeat until plants are set out in the field; examples include Actigard 50WG, Forum, Revus, Orondis, Presidio, Ranman 400 SC, Zampro, phosphonates (Aliette/Fosphite), Regalia, and biological controls (Cease, Double Nickel LC, LifeGard WG, Sonata, Stargus).

canonical.summary: Infection causes a brown, soft decay that destroys the plant crown tissue; older leaves wilt and eventually the entire plant wilts and collapses. Lower leaves wilt and drop to the soil surface, and where the leaf contacts the soil a white mycelium forms and sclerotia develop.

treatments: Crop rotation with non-hosts; for S. minor, crop rotations and deep inversion plowing may help reduce incidence.
Deep plowing to keep sclerotia from the soil surface.
Avoid known crop hosts including beans, cauliflower, celery, corn salad, endive, escarole, fennel, pepper, radicchio, and tomato.

Before disease appears, apply fungicides on a 14-day interval.
Example products: Iprodione (Rovral 4F), Cyprodinil/Fludioxonil (Switch 62.5WG), Boscalid (Endura), Fludioxonil (Cannonball WG), Dicloran (Botran).

canonical.summary: Blighted flower buds, brown and undersized foliage, wilted shoot tips, and scattered twig and small branch dieback; blossoms and the associated shoots wilt and die, and gum exudes at the base of infected flowers. Fruit infection first appears as small water-soaked lesions that rapidly expand to consume the entire fruit, and discolored decay spots develop on fruit and nuts.
diagnostic_features: Cankers on blighted twigs have tan centers with dark margins, and during foggy, humid, or rainy weather gray to tan velvety spore masses form on diseased blossoms and twig cankers. Shoots killed by brown rot turn mostly brown to tan (versus black for bacterial blast, which produces no visible spores). Diseased shriveled fruit may be held in the canopy as mummies, and stem cankers are accompanied by copious gum production (gummosis).
look_alikes: Bacterial blast, blight, and canker caused by the Pseudomonas syringae bacterium
Citrus brown rot caused by Phytophthora species
treatments: Where available, choose plant varieties that are resistant to brown rot, and keep trees vigorous with appropriate cultural care.
Remove infected leaves, shoots and fruit to reduce inoculum within and around the tree; promptly remove and dispose of diseased shoots during dry weather.
Prune branches (and thin interior branches of young trees) during dry weather to maintain an open canopy for better air circulation and sunlight penetration, which promotes drying.
After working on an infected tree, clean tools and dip or spray them with a 10% bleach solution, 70% isopropyl rubbing alcohol, or a commercial disinfectant.
Use drip or furrow irrigation or low-angle sprinklers to avoid wetting blossoms, foliage, and fruit.
Avoid overfertilizing with nitrogen, and manage other diseases and pests that wound fruit or nuts.
Inspect green fruit at least weekly and remove affected fruit before spores form; cool fruit quickly after harvest and inspect during storage.
Chemical control is based on protection of flower parts; time applications to each cultivar's bloom stage, treating at pink bud (5-10% bloom) and full bloom.
One application at full bloom is sufficient in most orchards in most years with low rainfall; a second or third near full bloom may be needed in severe years or extended wet bloom.

Begin applications just before buds open (pink or white color) and repeat at regular intervals per label; e.g., myclobutanil or thiophanate-methyl at 20-40% bloom, with a second application at 80-100% bloom if high humidity or heavy rainfall follow.

canonical.summary: White, powdery fungal growth develops on both leaf surfaces, petioles, and stems, usually first appearing on crown leaves, shaded lower leaves, and leaf undersurfaces, with yellow spots forming on upper leaf surfaces opposite the colonies; on watermelon, initial symptoms may appear as a reddish-brown, bronzed appearance on older leaves, and fruit can exhibit white powdery patches on the rind.
diagnostic_features: White, powdery fungal growth (asexual conidia) on both leaf surfaces, petioles, and stems, with yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces opposite the colonies; older plants affected first; dark brown chasmothecia about 0.003 inches in diameter develop late in the season.
treatments: Plant resistant varieties (select varieties with resistance from both parents/homozygous resistance when possible)
Choose planting sites with good air movement and free of shade; ensure adequate plant spacing
Separate successive cucurbit plantings physically (plant up-wind of older plantings) to prevent older plants from serving as an inoculum source
Remove debris, weeds (including citron watermelon), and volunteer plants that may harbor the pathogen
Scout fields routinely (particularly lower leaf surfaces) beginning at the start of crop development; early detection is key
Begin preventative fungicide applications when crops start producing fruit, when first female flowers open, or when powdery mildew is reported in the area
Apply fungicides on a 7 to 10-day interval before disease appears; initiate weekly spray program when symptoms are found
Apply fungicides before the epidemic reaches 10 to 25% severity for best efficacy
Alternate products with different modes of action / FRAC codes to avoid fungicide-resistant strains; apply mobile/systemic fungicides together with a protectant contact fungicide (tank mix)
Use translaminar or systemic fungicides that move to the lower leaf surface
DMI fungicides (FRAC Code 3): Proline, Procure, Luna Experience, Rhyme, Aprovia Top, Inspire Super, Mettle, Rally (Myclobutanil)
Carboxamide / SDHI fungicides (FRAC Code 7): Aprovia Top, Luna fungicides, Miravis Prime
Quinoxyfen (Quintec) and Cyflufenamid (Torino) — apply at most once based on resistance testing
Metrafenone (Vivando, FRAC Code 50/U8) — exhibited excellent control in evaluations
Gatten (FRAC Code U13)
Pyraclostrobin + boscalid (Pristine); Azoxystrobin + difenoconazole (Quadris Top)
Protectant fungicides: chlorothalonil (Bravo Weather Stik), sulfur, copper, mineral oil (mancozeb is not effective for powdery mildew)
Sulfur is one of the most effective and least expensive products

Biopesticides for organic production: botanical oils, bicarbonates, hydrogen dioxide, microbes (biocontrol agents); fixed copper formulations are the only OMRI-labeled active ingredients with some efficacy
Home gardeners: products containing copper or chlorothalonil (e.g., Daconil); grow varieties with tolerance

canonical.summary: Small orange to yellow raised spots (spermagonia) develop on the upper leaf surface in spring, surrounded by larger yellowish orange pustules (aecia) near the ground; orange to yellow pustules (uredinia) appear on the leaf underside in June and July and later darken to black teliospores.
diagnostic_features: The appearance of aecia on the top of leaves early in the growing season generally distinguishes yellow rust from late leaf rust; season of appearance and which caneberry types are affected help distinguish the rust, though expert spore examination may be required.
treatments: Grow raspberries where they will receive full sun.
Plant them on a raised berm or mound of soil to improve air circulation around the plants.
Remove any wild caneberries near those grown for fruit because they can be alternative hosts from which the pathogen can spread.
Control weeds to improve air circulation and reduce humidity around plants.
Any method of pruning and trellising that improves air circulation around caneberries helps to reduce yellow rust.
The dry conditions in a macrotunnel (hoop house covered with clear plastic) greatly limit yellow rust if the tunnels are constructed before environmental conditions favor rust infections.
After harvest, cultivate to bury debris or dispose of it away from caneberries.
Remove fruiting canes after harvest.
Complete removal of floricanes and the first flush of primocane helps to control this disease because it removes most sources of pathogen inoculum
Stripping leaves from primocanes in the fall will also reduce overwintering inoculum.
spraying Bordeaux mixture or another copper fungicide may be warranted during the delayed dormant season, which is once buds appear and swell before they open
a fixed copper fungicide or myclobutanil can be sprayed during the first bloom

Avoid overhead irrigation that keeps trees wet for extended periods

Replace with a resistant clone, as susceptibility varies greatly between clones of the same species

Chemical control in spring as leaves flush and wet weather is forecast, applied before rainfall: e.g., Armada 50 WDG (3-9 oz/100 gal, Group 3+11), Daconil Weather Stik (1.38 pints/100 gal at budbreak, Group M5), Heritage (1-4 oz/100 gal, Group 11), Protect DF (1-2 lb/100 gal), Spectro 90 WDG (1-2 lb/100 gal, Group 1+M5)

canonical.summary: Yellow foliage appears on one or more branches in the outer crown from late spring to midsummer, soon becoming wilted and brown ("flagging"), with yellowing and wilting progressing down the infected branch toward the trunk; fallen leaves may be strewn over the lawn in spring or summer.
diagnostic_features: Wilted and brown foliage on individual branches called "flagging," with brown discoloration/streaking of the sapwood visible when the bark is removed on recently wilted branches.
treatments: Manage by eliminating bark beetle breeding sites: promptly remove dead or dying elm wood with intact bark.
Remove DED-infected branches the same year infection starts, before the disease moves into the main stem, cutting at least 5 feet (preferably 10 feet) below the last sign of streaking in the sapwood.
Properly dispose of elm wood by burying, debarking, burning, or chipping.
Sever root grafts between infected and adjacent elms (e.g., with a vibratory plow or trenching to 3-4 feet deep) before removing the infected tree.
Take down trees with many infected branches.
Choose Dutch elm disease-resistant cultivars for new or replacement plantings.
Preventative fungicide injection treatments (e.g., thiabendazole, propiconazole) can protect highly valuable trees, but are expensive and regarded as a temporary measure.
Without community-wide sanitation, Dutch elm disease is almost impossible to control.

canonical.summary: White mold first appears as pale, often bleached, water-soaked (watery) rot lesions on stems, leaves, and pods; white threadlike, cottony mycelium is often visible on rotted tissue under moist conditions, after which affected tissue dries and bleaches to a pale tan, beige, or almost white color and black sclerotia develop.
diagnostic_features: The development of black, irregularly shaped (round to oblong) sclerotiaâ€”compact masses of myceliaâ€”within the white cottony fungal growth is the best diagnostic feature; sclerotia are white early in development and turn black when fully developed, formed on plant surfaces and inside pods or stems, while affected tissue dries quickly and bleaches to a pale tan, beige, or almost white color.
treatments: Rotate with non-host crops (small grains, corn, rye, wheat, grasses, cereals) for at least 2-3 years, and up to 3-8 years, to reduce soil inoculum and sclerotia populations.
Use wide row spacing (36 inches recommended) to increase air movement and promote drying of the soil and plant canopy.
Use management practices that reduce heavy canopies and increase air movement.
Avoid heavy applications of nitrogen / over-fertilization, which can produce excessive, dense, lush canopies.

Plant erect, upright, open-canopy (open-base) varieties that hold pods off the ground and do not produce excessive foliage near ground level; resistant bean varieties (including dry bean types) are available.
Orient bean rows in the direction of the prevailing winds to promote air drainage and drying of plant and soil surfaces.
Avoid planting the most susceptible crops in fields surrounded by dense woods that restrict air circulation.
Time irrigations to allow drying of the plant canopy before nightfall and avoid excessive irrigation after petal fall.
Plant garbanzo beans later (December through early February) rather than early (early November) to avoid heavy canopies that increase humidity.
Scout and inspect plants for symptoms beginning at emergence/bloom, keeping written notes and photographic records of occurrence and severity.
Practice good weed control, removing susceptible weeds (in particular ragweed) from the field.
Avoid wounds and remove affected plants.
Incorporate debris promptly after harvest and use deep plowing to bury sclerotia and reduce sclerotia production.
Field flooding during warm temperatures destroys sclerotia.
Use a timely harvest with rapid cooling and pod storage at 45Â°F to 50Â°F for effective postharvest control.

Apply foliar fungicides starting at early bloom (1% to 10% bloom) in fields with a history of white mold, obtaining thorough coverage with high water volume (50 gallons per acre minimum) and high pressure (100 to 200 psi).
Conventional fungicides in FRAC groups 1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 12 and 29 are labeled for white mold, in addition to contact fungicides copper and chlorothalonil.
BOSCALID (Endura) at 8 to 11 oz/A at the beginning of flowering and again at full bloom.
THIOPHANATE METHYL (Topsin M WSB at 1 to 1.5 lb/A; T-Methyl 4.5F AG / Topsin 4.5 FL at 30 to 40 fl oz/A).
Blocker 4F (Group 14) at 4 pints/A at planting and again on 2- to 3-week intervals when disease is severe.
Botran 75W (Group 14) at 2 2/3 lb/A on 7-day intervals.
Cannonball WG (Group 12) at 7 oz/A when 10% of plants have at least one open blossom.
Fontelis at 16 to 30 fl oz/A at the beginning of flowering and again at full bloom.
Luna Privilege at 6.84 fl oz/A on 14-day intervals.
Rovral 4 Flowable at 1.5 to 2 pints/A when 10% of plants have at least one open bloom.
Omega 500F (Group 29) at 0.5 to 0.85 pint/A when 10% to 30% of plants have at least one open blossom.
Switch 62.5WG (Group 12 + 9) at 11 to 14 oz/A.
Jet-Ag at 0.75 to 3.9 fl oz/5 gal water as a weekly preventative treatment.
Biological/soil treatments: Contans WG (a parasitic fungus that attacks sclerotia) at 1 to 4 lb/A as a preplant or postharvest treatment.
Regalia Biofungicide (Group P5) at 1 to 4 quarts/A on 7- to 10-day intervals.
Double Nickel LC at 1 to 6 quarts/A at planting and again at cultivation.
Serenade Opti at 14 to 20 oz/A on 7- to 10-day intervals.
Stargus at 2 to 4 quarts/A plus a nonionic surfactant on 7- to 10-day intervals.

canonical.summary: Symptoms begin as small yellow or white slightly raised spots on leaf surfaces that enlarge into reddish-brown pustules (uredinia) about 1/8 inch or smaller; pustules may be surrounded by a yellow border and release rusty spores, and severe infection causes leaves to curl, dry, turn brown, and drop prematurely.
diagnostic_features: Rust can be distinguished from other foliar diseases because the rust-colored spores will rub off, while with other foliar diseases, nothing rubs off.
treatments: Rotate bean with non-host crops / rotate away from any bean for two years to remove sources of inoculum.
Plow under or bury infected crop residues and bean debris right after harvest.
Eliminate volunteer bean plants.
Plant within recommended planting periods (e.g. May 15 to June 15) to reduce late-season exposure to the pathogen.
Select planting dates and schedule irrigation to avoid long periods of leaf wetness when temperatures are warm (e.g. avoid foliage staying wet at night for more than 10 hours).
Plant rust-resistant cultivars (available for many market classes including pinto, great northern, small white, red kidney, and black beans), recognizing many races of the fungus exist.
Avoid over-application of nitrogen and ensure adequate potassium fertilization.
Disinfect poles used in pole-bean production.
Scout fields frequently during late vegetative to early pod development for initial rust pustules.

canonical.summary: Circular, tan to gray lesions develop on the lower leaves and stems of the plant, typically small (<1/8 in), with a dark-brown perimeter and often a yellow halo; small dark pycnidia may appear in the center of the lesion. Disease begins on lower leaves and progresses upward.

Disease progresses from older (lower) growth to younger (upper) growth.
treatments: Rotate away from tomato (or susceptible solanaceous crops) for 1-2 or more years
Control presence of horsenettle and other host weeds
Remove crop debris from planting areas (particularly tomato crop debris); destroy infested plant debris
Reduce the amount of time plants are wet, when possible; avoid over-irrigating
Stake or trellis plants to improve air circulation and drying of leaves
Use mulches or plastic to reduce contact between leaves and soil; mulch the garden to prevent watersplash
Avoid working in fields when leaves are wet
Scout plants often and remove infected plants/leaves
Clean tools and equipment after leaving a field; disinfect stakes and cages
Maintain proper spacing between plants
Plant resistant varieties
Remove 'suckers' or lowest lateral tomato plant growth
Use raised beds and rotate which bed has tomatoes from year to year

canonical.summary: Lesions appear on leaves and fruit as light green circular spots that become olive green and velvety, later darkening and becoming scabby; severe infection causes leaf curling, puckering, and premature drop, and deformed cracked fruit.
diagnostic_features: Small, velvety, olive green lesions with unclear margins on the lower leaf surface that age into darker spots with more distinct margins; lesions may appear more numerous closer to the mid-vein of the leaf; on some crabapples, infections may be reddish in color.
treatments: Plant resistant or scab-immune apple varieties (e.g., Redfree, Prima, Liberty, Freedom, Jonafree, Macfree, Sir Prize, William's Pride, Enterprise, Gold Rush, Pristine) as the ideal method for managing scab.
Rake and destroy fallen leaves below apple and crabapple trees in the fall (or chop leaves with a mulching/flail mower).
Couple leaf chopping with two or three applications of 5 percent urea to fall foliage to speed leaf decomposition.
For new plantings, select a site with at least eight hours of direct sun and space trees so air moves easily through the canopies and orchard.
Prune trees yearly to open the canopy, increase air movement and sunlight penetration, and promote leaf drying.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
Where resistance is absent, apply protectant fungicides starting at green tip (first susceptible tissue) and continue on a 7- to 10-day schedule through petal fall and fruit development.
Use curative-action fungicides when a weather monitoring system identifies that an infection period has occurred.
Apply cover sprays during the summer only if primary-season scab control was inadequate.
Organic and backyard growers can use biocontrol products to suppress disease development, combined with resistant varieties for maximum control.

canonical.summary: Water-soaked, oily areas with yellow halos on cotyledons that become dark angular necrotic patches; small dark angled lesions on mature leaves; and a dark green stain or blotch on the upper surface of developing fruit that rapidly expands to cover the entire fruit and causes rind rupture.
diagnostic_features: The diagnostic symptom of BFB is a dark green stain or blotch on the upper surface of the developing fruit that may be 0.5 inch in diameter at first but will rapidly expand to cover the entire fruit surface within a week.
look_alikes: other less harmful bacteria that can produce identical symptoms on seedling plants
treatments: Practice good greenhouse sanitation: Use a 10 percent bleach solution or Physan 20 to dip all tools, recycled planting trays, and containers for at least 10 minutes.
Spray benches and the interior with the same solution.
Remove any weeds growing in the greenhouse.
Water plants evenly in early morning or by afternoon.
Bottom watering of transplants will help control BFB.
Purchase watermelon seed that has been tested negative for bacterial fruit blotch in a seedling grow-out test.
Monitor transplants for symptoms.
Try to segregate triploid seedless varieties and seed lots from diploid seeded varieties in the greenhouse.
Reduce physical contact with the seedlings.
If suspicious symptoms are observed, remove infected plants and have them diagnosed immediately for bacterial fruit blotch.
If transplants are confirmed to have BFB, destroy all transplants from that seed lot.
A greenhouse with infected transplants can be decontaminated and planted the following season.
If infected plants or potentially infected plants have been transplanted in the field, begin copper spray applications to suppress BFB.
Copper hydroxide fungicides can be tank mixed with most fungicides used to control fungal diseases.
If symptoms are observed, copper hydroxide should be applied immediately after planting on a 7- to 10-day schedule.
If no symptoms are observed but BFB is suspected, copper hydroxide should be applied when the first male flowers appear.
Continue spray applications until all fruit have reached maturity.
Fields should not be cultivated or sprayed when the foliage is wet.
If BFB has occurred, follow a strict three-year rotation, deep plow after harvest and control all volunteer melons and cucurbit weeds.

Eradicate nearby fire blight hosts such as pyracantha, hawthorn, cotoneaster, and crabapple
Avoid excessive irrigation and avoid wetting foliage with sprinkler irrigation
Protect open blossoms during high-risk warm/wet weather

canonical.summary: Characteristic foliar symptoms include chlorosis and necrosis between leaf veins, followed by leaf curling and leaf death; externally infected stems look healthy but split stems show internal browning of vascular tissue and pith, especially at nodes and in the lower stem.
diagnostic_features: When stems are split lengthwise, internal browning of vascular tissue and pith is evident, especially at nodes and in the lower stem (pith is white in healthy stems); pith color in the lower stem differentiates BSR from sudden death syndrome (SDS).
treatments: Use resistant soybean varieties (the most efficient way to manage BSR)
Crop rotation to non-host crops such as corn, small grains, and forage legumes will reduce pathogen levels
Many soybean varieties with PI 88788-derived SCN resistance also have BSR resistance, so SCN resistance may also help reduce BSR

canonical.summary: Yellowing/chlorosis of leaf margins followed by light- to dark-brown necrotic spots on cotyledons and leaves; ovate stem and vine cankers near nodes that crack and exude a characteristic brown/amber gummy fluid; fruit lesions begin as water-soaked spots that develop into large brown to black depressed spots (black rot).
diagnostic_features: Black fungal fruiting bodies (pycnidia, perithecia, or pseudothecia) on infected leaves, stems, and fruits; pycnidia swell and release tendrils of spores when wetted; stem and vine lesions near nodes that exude a characteristic brown/amber gummy substance; raised, black, pimple-like spore-producing structures within the black areas of fruit rot.
treatments: Purchase seeds or seedlings free of pathogens from a reputable company with a good history of GSB-free seed production
Use treated seed; disinfectant solutions are more effective than dry-dust seed treatments
Plant resistant varieties where available (watermelon, pumpkin, buttercup, and canary melons have resistant cultivars)
Routinely inspect transplant seedlings in greenhouses and dispose of all seedlings near infected plants; do not use healthy-looking seedlings from trays containing infected plants
Rotate crops with non-host plants such as small grains or corn for at least 2-4 years, removing all volunteer cucurbits
Eradicate wild citrons, balsam pear, and other volunteer cucurbits/weeds before planting
Decaying crop debris should be disked and deep-plowed into the soil post-harvest to speed decomposition and reduce overwintering inoculum
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers; if watering by hand, water at the base of the stem
In small gardens, remove and destroy infected fruit and vines at the end of the season
Use integrated pest management to control cucumber beetles and other insect pests, as well as powdery mildew
Avoid wounding fruits during harvest, and store fruits at 45 F-50 F to prevent postharvest black rot
Apply fungicides preventatively; effective contact fungicides include chlorothalonil and mancozeb, and there are many effective systemic fungicides
Alternate fungicide chemistries during the spray program to prevent fungicide resistance

canonical.summary: Yellowing of leaves and unthrifty growth, with affected bines wilting rapidly and suddenly (often at flowering or in hot weather); the bine base is typically swollen and may have a longitudinal split, and bines detach easily from the crown.
diagnostic_features: Swollen bine base with a narrow, tapered/rounded point of attachment to the crown (only a few central vascular elements connect bine to crown), bines that break off with a gentle tug, sometimes a longitudinal split in the cortical area, and an absence of vascular discoloration.
treatments: Avoid injury to hop plants.
Chemical pruning in the spring reduced canker disease severity compared to mechanical pruning, but no difference was detected in Oregon field studies.
Hilling up the plants enhances adventitious root growth above cankered bine portions, which can help maintain bine vigor and cone yield.
Reduce crown wetness by hilling higher relative to rill irrigation ditches, by removing sucker growth that could shade the crown, and by reducing mulch.
Lime to increase soil pH above 7.
Maintain the higher pH by using less ammonium-based nitrogen fertilizer; use nitrate-based fertilizer instead.
Mefenoxam applications are not an effective chemical treatment for Fusarium canker based on studies by OSU.
Asperello at 1.5 to 10.7 oz/A on 7- to 10-day intervals as a foliar spray or at 0.1 to 0.7 oz/100 gal water on 8- to 12-week intervals for chemigation at 2,000 to 5,000 gal/A.
Bio-Tam 2 at 2.5 to 3 lb/A as a banded ground spray or at 2.5 to 5 lb/A on 14- to 21-day intervals for chemigation.
Bexfond at 7 to 14 fl oz/A for soil applications via drenches, in-furrow applications, drip irrigation, or sprays, followed by irrigation, reapply on 4-week intervals.
Theia at 1 to 5 lb/A for soil applications via drenches, in-furrow applications, drip irrigation, or sprays, followed by irrigation.

summary.quote: Canker disease leads to yellowing of leaves and generally unthrifty growth. Affected bines wilt rapidly and suddenly; often at flowering or during hot weather. Bines can detach and readily break from the crown with a gentle tug.

The bine's base is typically swollen because carbohydrate movement has been inhibited; sometimes affected stems have a longitudinal split in the colonized cortical area of the bine. Vascular discoloration does not seem to be associated with the disease.

canonical.summary: Yellowish-green blotches appear near leaf tips on older leaves, enlarging and changing to shades of red to purple in oats, yellow to red in wheat, and bright yellow in barley, often with dwarfing and stunting.
diagnostic_features: Reddish-purple or yellowish discoloration of the flag leaf is the most characteristic symptom; symptoms appear patchy in a field due to aphid vector movement and are most apparent when days are cool and light intensity is high; does not produce a distinct mosaic pattern.
treatments: Plant BYDV-resistant or tolerant cultivars (resistance is more available in oats than in wheat and barley); grow diverse varieties.
Delay fall seeding of winter wheat until aphid populations decline; plant winter wheat after the Hessian fly-free date; plant spring oats as early as possible.
Control grassy weeds and volunteer cereals (wheat, barley, oats) within and near production fields to eliminate the green bridge for aphids.
Avoid planting small grains in midsummer as cover or companion crops in wheat-producing areas.
Seed treatments with imidacloprid (Gaucho) or thiamethoxam (Cruiser) can reduce fall aphid populations and primary infections.
Foliar contact or systemic insecticides may be used against aphids in the fall, though insecticide use is generally not economically beneficial due to sporadic aphid movement.
Maintain proper fertilization for good crop growth.

Repeat fungicide sprays yearly until symptoms have disappeared

Rubbing fingers across the leaf blade yields yellow powdery residues.
treatments: Become familiar with stripe rust symptoms and anticipate environmental conditions conducive for the disease; check fields periodically and early in the season.
Use of resistant varieties is the best way to control wheat losses to stripe rust.

canonical.summary: Many tiny yellow spots appear on both upper and lower surfaces of current-season needles in late summer to autumn, most abundant near the needle apex; spots enlarge and darken over winter, and by spring coalesce into characteristic dark reddish-brown (deep red-brown, mottled) blotches, causing needle browning and premature defoliation, with diseased needles typically cast by late June.
diagnostic_features: Fruiting bodies (apothecia) appear on each side of the midrib on the needle's lower surface; the needle's epidermis lifts up as a patch and splits open, exposing an orange to orange-brown fungus structure. The disease often initiates and is most severe in the lower canopy, and diseased needles are typically cast (dropped) by late June.
treatments: Thoroughly scout trees for disease symptoms from autumn through early spring, prior to bud break
On small trees, prune and destroy diseased branches; prune out heavily infected shoots/branches from the lower canopy and remove severely infected trees to prevent spread
In Christmas tree plantations, remove and destroy any infected trees
Avoid overhead watering while new foliage is growing
Do not plant in areas with poor air drainage / low-lying areas; if the location is exposed to shade during the day, do not plant Douglas-fir
Space trees properly and prune the lowest canopy branches to promote air flow and good air circulation
Remove weeds around the base of trees, thin canopy, and avoid establishing ground cover plantings to reduce humidity and lingering moisture
Avoid using east-side and Rocky Mountain seed sources; in disease-prone or marginal sites use seed sources with partial resistance (among the most resistant: Shuswap and Pillar Lake)

Apply fungicides with thorough coverage of all needles; make first application when new growth is 1 to 2 inches long (or once 50% of buds have broken and new growth reaches 0.5 inch) and an additional application 3 weeks later â€” three applications are usually required for good control

Fungicides include: chlorothalonil, copper-based products (copper hydroxide, copper sulfate, copper salts of fatty and/or rosin acids), mancozeb-based products, thiophanate-methyl, azoxystrobin (Heritage/Quadris), and thiophanate-methyl + chlorothalonil mixtures (Spectro 90 WDG), Tourney EZ

canonical.summary: Early season symptoms include seed rot and pre- and postemergence damping off. At seedling and later vegetative stages, infected stems appear bruised and soft with a dark chocolate-brown discoloration extending from below the soil line upward into lower parts of the plant, often reaching several nodes and girdling the stem; secondary roots rot, leaves turn yellow and wilt, plants may be stunted and chlorotic, and are often killed in patches or in sections of rows with wilted leaves typically staying attached after plant death.
diagnostic_features: A dark chocolate-brown lesion on the lower stem extending from below the soil line upward from the taproot, often reaching several nodes and girdling the stem; wilted leaves typically remain attached after plant death; plants killed in patches or sections of rows.
treatments: Plant resistant cultivars; widely effective Rps resistance genes include Rps 1c and 1k, with Rps 1a, Rps 3 and others also effective in some regions
Where Rps genes are overcome by local pathogen races, plant cultivars with high levels of field tolerance (partial resistance, polygenic)
Create field environment that reduces the likelihood of saturated soil by improving drainage where possible
Use seed treatments or soil-applied fungicides targeting oomycetes; mefenoxam (Apron XL) or metalaxyl (Apron) at the highest labeled rates are effective
Crop rotation and tillage may be of some benefit

treatments.quote: Try to create a field environment that reduces the likelihood of saturated soil by taking steps to increase drainage where possible. Treatment of seed with the highest labeled rates of fungicidal compounds such as mefenoxam (Apron XL®) or metalaxyl (Apron®) can be beneficial. In all areas where Phytophthora root and stem rot has been a problem, resistant cultivars should be planted. The most common resistance genes that are widely effective are Rps 1c and 1k. Rps1a can be effective, but is not as effective in many areas as the other genes. Rps 3 and other genes can also be effective. For areas where the Rps genes are not working well due to the presence of pathogen races that overcome the resistance, cultivars with high levels of field tolerance (or partial resistance) should be planted. Crop rotation and tillage may be of some benefit.

canonical.summary: Infections begin as small, angular, water-soaked spots that turn yellow and then brown as the tissue dies, surrounded by yellowish-green halos; spots often merge into large irregular dead patches, and the dead tissue may fall out giving leaves a ragged or tattered appearance.
diagnostic_features: Distinguished from Septoria brown spot by the presence of a yellow/yellowish-green halo around lesions and by the absence of fungal structures within lesions; bacterial blight is most common on young leaves in the upper canopy, whereas brown spot is typically seen on older, lower leaves.
treatments: Plant resistant soybean varieties / cultivars not highly susceptible to the disease
Use pathogen-free (certified) seed
Rotate with non-host crops (alfalfa, corn, small grains)
Incorporate crop residue via tillage to reduce bacterial survival in debris (deep tillage in chronically affected fields)
Avoid field cultivation when foliage is wet to prevent spread
Copper fungicides labeled for bacterial blight, applied early in the disease cycle

canonical.summary: Common rust produces rust-colored to dark brown, elongated pustules on both leaf surfaces; the pustules contain cinnamon brown rust spores (urediniospores) and darken as they age, with leaf chlorosis and death possible under severe conditions.
diagnostic_features: Brown pustules occur on both the top and bottom leaf surfaces, which differentiates common rust from Southern rust.
treatments: Plant resistant or moderately resistant corn hybrids/cultivars — the best and most cost-effective management practice; use moderately resistant cultivars for late-season plantings.
Apply fungicides, especially early when few pustules have appeared on the leaves; in sweet corn, fungicides are typically applied at V7-V8 and tassel.
Use fungicides containing strobilurins (FRAC Group 11) and demethylation inhibitors (FRAC Group 3) for adequate control.
For common rust, spray fungicide when 80% of observed leaves have one or more pustules.
Scout fields early and frequently when corn rust is found nearby to prepare for potential fungicide applications.
If irrigation is used, apply it at midday to minimize the time leaves are wet, reducing infection and disease spread.
Use crop rotation of at least three years between field or sweet corn crops (manages other foliar diseases, though it will not influence common rust severity).

canonical.summary: Initial gray to white lesions develop at the nodes (R3 to R6), rapidly progressing above and below the nodes and sometimes girdling the stem; white, fluffy mold soon covers the infected area, especially during periods of high relative humidity. Leaf tissue between major veins turns a gray-green cast and eventually leaves die and turn completely brown while remaining attached to the stem.
diagnostic_features: Fluffy white mold growth on stems with characteristic black sclerotia (hard, irregular, with a pink to white center, resembling rodent droppings) embedded in the mold on stem lesions and inside the stem; wilted dead leaves remain attached to stems; affected pods contain smaller, lighter, white, cottony seeds that may be replaced by sclerotia.
look_alikes: Bird's nest fungi (can be confused with white mold apothecia)
treatments: Select cultivars with high levels of partial resistance and an open canopy of upright leaves (no soybean variety is completely resistant)
Long-term crop rotation (2-3+ years) with non-host crops such as corn and wheat to minimize inoculum build-up; avoid rotation with beans, peas, sunflowers, and cole crops (Brassicaceae)
Tillage (moldboard plowing) to bury sclerotia at least 10 cm for fields with first occurrence; reduced tillage for fields with a long history of the disease
Reduce seeding rate and increase row spacing (e.g., 30-inch rows) to improve air circulation and avoid complete canopy closure
Where irrigation is used, reduce irrigation frequency during flowering
Weed control, as many broadleaf weeds are hosts of the pathogen

Foliar fungicides applied immediately before infection (timing is critical); boscalid has shown good efficacy; avoid thiophanate methyl and strobilurin fungicides such as pyraclostrobin; rotate active ingredients
Herbicides such as lactofen to modify soybean canopy, delay flowering, and induce systemic acquired resistance; some herbicides may also suppress the fungus or disrupt germination of sclerotia
Biological control with the fungus Coniothyrium minitans, incorporated to a depth of about 2 inches (5 cm)

Use Sclerotinia-free seed; clean seed lots with spiral separators and gravity tables; apply seed treatments with fungicides for infected seed; avoid harvesting heavily infested fields until end of season

affected_parts.quote: Lesions usually develop first at stem nodes during or after flowering. The lesions expand and the tops of the plants become grayish-green and then wilt and die. Infected stems often become soft and watery, and become covered with white moldy growth in moist conditions. Dry, dead stems can develop a bleached, white appearance. Hard, black sclerotia that look similar to rodent droppings develop on or inside infected stems and pods. ... Seed lots can be contaminated with sclerotia, and seeds can be infected with the pathogen.

canonical.summary: Irregularly shaped, water-soaked leaf spots that appear angular because they are bounded by the leaf veins; bacteria may ooze from the spots in droplets that dry to a white residue, the area later turns gray and dies, and dead tissue often tears away leaving large irregular holes. Fruit lesions are smaller, circular, and superficial.
diagnostic_features: The spots expand until limited by larger veins, which gives them an angular appearance; under humid conditions the water-soaked spots are covered by a white exudate (bacterial ooze) that dries to a thin, white crust on or adjacent to the spot on the underleaf surface; as spots dry they tear away leaving large, irregular holes.
treatments: Plant certified, pathogen-free (clean, bacteria-free) seed; if saving seed, do not collect seed from infected plants.
Plant resistant/tolerant varieties (many resistant cucumber varieties are available).
Hot water seed treatment can remove some, but not all, bacteria (not fully effective alone).
Rotate out of cucurbits for 2 or more years (do not grow cucurbits in the same field more than once every three or four years) and avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization.
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers; if watering by hand, water at the base of the plant.
Do not cultivate, harvest, or work in plants when leaves are wet, and stay out of wet, infected fields.
Remove and destroy infected fruit and vines at the end of the season; in large fields till in or plow under infected debris to speed decomposition.
Apply copper-based bactericides early (e.g., fixed-copper products, Badge SC, Cueva, Kocide, Previsto) at first sign of disease; sprays are not effective once disease is severe.
Apply Actigard 50WG (Group P1) at 0.5 to 1 oz/A on 7-day intervals.
Tank-mix the recommended bactericide with effective fungicides to also protect against fungal diseases.

treatments: Rotate soybean with non-hosts such as wheat or corn

canonical.summary: Irregularly shaped pale green to light yellow spots appear on upper leaf surfaces, enlarging into pale to bright yellow spots; older lesions turn brown with yellow-green margins and eventually become necrotic spots; fuzzy, gray tufts may be visible on the leaf underside.
diagnostic_features: Fuzzy, gray tufts (sporulation) growing from lesions on the leaf underside, particularly when humidity is high or leaves are wet (e.g., early in the morning); infected seeds may be smaller, dull white, with cracks in the seed coat, and the inside of the pod can be covered with a dried, whitish crusty fungal mass.
treatments: Plant resistant varieties — many sources of resistance are available
Crop rotation
Burial of infested crop residue to reduce pathogen levels
Typically no fungicide management is warranted; most foliar fungicides available for soybeans are not labeled for downy mildew and have very limited effect

canonical.summary: Pre- and postemergence damping off occurs; infected seedlings show sunken, firm, dry reddish-brown (rusty-brown) lesions on the hypocotyls/stems and roots near the soil line; lateral roots may decay; plants may become stunted, yellow, and may wilt, and may remain stunted even if they grow out of root rot.
diagnostic_features: Sunken, firm, dry rusty/reddish-brown lesions on stems (hypocotyls) and roots near the soil line; lesions can girdle the stem and kill or stunt plants.
treatments: Encourage seedling health with good agronomic practices and the use of high quality seed
Avoid or reduce plant stress, for example from herbicide injury and SCN infection
Crop rotation and tillage may be of value where disease has been severe

canonical.summary: Round, tan lesions with dark purple to brown margins appear on leaves, bearing small black pycnidia; infected berries turn brown and soft then become hard, black, shriveled mummies dotted with pycnidia.
diagnostic_features: Tiny black dots (pycnidia) appear in the lesion, usually in a ring pattern near the border of the lesion; lesions on shoots, cluster stems, rachises and tendrils are oval, sunken and purple to black; infected berries shrivel into hard raisin-like mummies that remain attached to the cluster.
treatments: Sanitation is the most important element of management; remove infected canes, spurs, and fruit clusters remaining on the vines
Rake up and dispose of fallen leaves and mummies
Use mulch or cultivate beneath the vines prior to bud break to bury mummies and reduce initial inoculum
Drop mummies remaining in the canopy to the ground and bury them at the end of the season
Prune out diseased/infected canes and tendrils during the dormant season; remove leaf lesions and diseased fruit when first observed
Reduce humidity in the canopy by removing canes or leaves and managing weeds
Select a sunny planting site with good air movement and orient rows with the prevailing winds so plants dry quickly
Provide proper vine spacing, maintain an open canopy, and maintain good weed control
Plant resistant or less susceptible varieties, hybrids, and Vitis species
Apply protectant fungicides (sulfur/Bordeaux mix, copper, mancozeb, or ferbam) beginning shortly before bloom and repeat through approximately 4-6 weeks post bloom with thorough coverage
Use systemic fungicides (strobilurins, sterol inhibitors) for later infections and kickback activity, rotating among chemical classes
Time fungicides from early bloom through three to four weeks after bloom, targeting the pre-bloom peak in spore production
Use disease forecasting models to predict periods of high disease pressure

canonical.summary: Characteristic mosaic pattern of chlorosis and necrosis on the upper surfaces of cucurbit leaves, with gray sporangia giving a fuzzy or downy appearance on the underside of leaves.
diagnostic_features: Leaf spots are angular and bounded by leaf veins (most distinct in cucumbers). Dark purplish-grey fuzz forms on the underside of the leaf in high humidity. On watermelons, an exaggerated upward leaf curling is common.
treatments: Early planting so fruit can be harvested before the pathogen arrives (downy mildew arrives in New York between July 4 and August 31).
Plant resistant cultivars; newer cucumber varieties with some resistance to cucurbit downy mildew are commercially available.
Track the spread of cucurbit downy mildew through the IPM Pest Information Platform for Extension and Education (ipmPIPE) at cdm.ipmpipe.org to time fungicide applications.

Apply chemical treatments per current recommendations (e.g., Cornell Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; Midwest Vegetable Production Guide). Rotate products to manage resistance.
Use drip irrigation and wide row spacing to dry the leaves and encourage good air movement around the plants.
Trellis plants to improve air circulation.
Remove plants with symptoms of disease.
Monitor plants for symptoms of disease, especially from August through harvest.

profiles.disease: Loose Smut Of Wheat Or Barley

canonical.summary: Mild symptoms may include yellowish leaf streaks and stiff, dark green leaves before heading; affected plants head out early producing sterile heads with clumped, sooty olive-black spores in place of healthy glumes and kernels, with only a bare rachis remaining after spore dispersal.
diagnostic_features: Spores are not enclosed by the seed coat, so are quickly dispersed by rain or wind, leaving only a bare rachis with a few fragments of glumes or awns; loose smut spores will NOT have a fishy odor.
treatments: Less susceptible varieties of wheat are available.
Plant certified seed to reduce disease risk.
Do not save seed from fields with loose smut.
Fungicide seed treatments can effectively manage loose smut.

canonical.summary: Dark-colored, irregularly-shaped, angular spots or blotches occurring primarily along the midrib, primary veins and leaf margins; vein-associated lesions, discrete necrotic spots, and irregular necrotic blotches or blights, with acervuli produced in the necrotic spots. Severely diseased trees can defoliate early.
diagnostic_features: Lesions occur along the midrib, primary veins and leaf margins (rather than randomly across the leaf) and vary by host: narrow purplish-black streaks along leaf veins on Norway maple, large brown blotches along primary veins on sugar maple, and tan or black lesions along primary veins and leaf margins on Japanese maple.
treatments: Avoid overhead irrigation of ornamental maples to reduce free moisture on the foliage; time irrigation to minimize the time leaves are wet
Remove infected leaves (the primary source of inoculum) from the site; rake up and destroy fallen leaves before the first snowfall
If the disease is severe, prune out infected shoots; remove and destroy twig cankers during dormant pruning
Maintain tree vigor through adequate fertilization, watering, mulching and pruning; reduce stress with adequate watering throughout the growing season
Redirect sprinklers that splash water on the tree's leaves
Do not fertilize unless a soil test shows the need; apply lime if soil pH is too low (sugar maple prefers calcareous soils)
Prune to increase light penetration and improve air circulation; avoid dense plantings in nurseries
Plant disease-resistant trees where possible

Apply labeled fungicides at or just before bud break to protect new growth; active ingredients include copper hydroxide + mancozeb, thiabendazole, mancozeb, propiconazole, thiophanate-methyl, and chlorothalonil

canonical.summary: Black rot causes large brown rotten areas on fruit (often with concentric rings), 'frog-eye' leaf spots with purplish/reddish edges and tan interiors, and sunken reddish-brown cankers on branches.
diagnostic_features: There is usually one spot per fruit (distinguishing it from bitter rot); leaf lesions show purple margins with brown/tan centers giving a 'frogeye' appearance; decayed flesh is not cone-shaped (unlike bitter rot); concentric bands of mahogany brown to black alternating with brown bands form on rotted fruit; small black pycnidia appear in the centers of leaf lesions.
treatments: Practice good sanitation: prune out dead or diseased branches, pick all dried and shriveled (mummified) fruit remaining on the trees, and remove infected plant material from the area (burn, bury, or send to municipal composting).
Prune correctly during dormancy (below 32 F; Feb-Mar in Minnesota); first prune out all dead branches, then prune to shape the tree.
Prune and remove cankers at least 15 inches below the basal end; properly dispose of prunings by burial or burning.
Take good care of trees: choose an appropriate site, plant only hardy cultivars, provide adequate water, and maintain tree health to prevent stress.
Control fire blight by pruning out infected wood or controlling insect vectors; remove limbs or trees killed by fire blight to discourage black rot.
Fungicide sprays are usually not needed in Minnesota; Captan and sulfur products labeled for scab also control black rot.
Captan and fungicides containing a strobilurin (FRAC Group 11) as an active ingredient are effective in controlling black rot on fruit.

canonical.summary: Early-season shoot blight produces patches of soft brown tissue and death of infected plant parts, with infections in leaf axils causing shoots to wilt or break off. At veraison, individually infected berries turn brown on white cultivars or reddish in red and black cultivars, and epidermal cracks develop fungal growth with a characteristic gray, velvety appearance.
diagnostic_features: Epidermal cracks form in which fungal growth produces mycelium and spores, resulting in the characteristic gray, velvety appearance of infected berries; under high humidity infected berries become covered with a gray growth of fungus mycelium.
treatments: Promote good air circulation and light penetration by proper pruning, controlling weeds and suckers, and positioning or removing shoots for uniform leaf development.
Where possible, rows should be planted in the direction of the prevailing wind.
Removal of leaves around clusters (or basal leaves immediately after berry set) before bunch closing reduces losses caused by Botrytis.
Canopy management practices such as shoot thinning, hedging, and leaf removal can be used to manage canopy density when appropriate.
Design vineyards to the anticipated vigor of the site to produce balanced canopies with moderate shoot vigor that optimize leaf and cluster exposure.
Prevent wounding by controlling insects, birds, and other grape diseases; manage insect populations that produce entry wounds.
Avoid unnecessary irrigation or nitrogen fertilization that may promote excessive canopy growth.

Apply effective fungicides at appropriate times: between bloom and pea-size berries if the canopy interior remains dry, otherwise before rainfall at bloom or after veraison; treat late-harvest grapes prior to bunch closure and as needed before harvest.
Alternate fungicides with different modes of action within and between seasons to prevent fungicide resistance.
Use resistant cultivars when practical.
Organically acceptable methods: canopy/cultural management plus sprays of Organic JMS Stylet Oil and Serenade.

Conventional fungicide options include CYPRODINIL (Vangard WG), FENHEXAMID (Elevate 50WDG), PYRIMETHANIL (Scala SC), FLUOPYRAM + TEBUCONAZOLE (Luna Experience), CYPRODINIL + FLUDIOXONIL (Switch 62.5WG), DIFENOCONAZOLE + CYPRODINIL (Inspire Super), IPRODIONE (Rovral 4F), PYRACLOSTROBIN + BOSCALID (Pristine), NARROW RANGE OIL (JMS Stylet), BACILLUS SUBTILIS (Serenade Max), ISOFETAMID (Kenja 400SC).

canonical.summary: Circular to angular leaf spots about 1/8 to 1/4 inch (3-6 mm) in diameter, brown to gray with dark reddish brown, purplish, or nearly black borders, which may converge to cover much of the leaf surface. On Bigleaf and panicle hydrangea the spots first appear on the bottom leaves; on oakleaf hydrangea the infected areas are more angular and dark brown to purple.
diagnostic_features: Spots roughly 1/8 to 1/4 inch in diameter with a pale or light brown center and dark margins (a frogeye pattern); the disease progresses from the bottom foliage to the top, and spores may eventually become visible as dark specks within the leaf spots.
treatments: Remove any diseased leaves that have fallen from the plant and hand-pick highly infected leaves from the plant.
Discard diseased leaves in the trash; do not put them in the compost bin.
Practice good sanitation to remove overwintering fungal inoculum; dispose of plant debris and infected leaves in the autumn.
Provide adequate plant spacing to increase air movement and sunlight penetration so leaves dry quickly.
Avoid practices that prevent leaves from drying quickly, such as overhead and excess watering; if foliage must be wetted, irrigate in the early morning.
Placement of hydrangeas in areas of lower light intensity may reduce infection.
Fertilize lightly with a nitrogen fertilizer to encourage new disease-free growth.

Apply labeled fungicides at the first onset of symptoms, e.g. chlorothalonil (Bonide Fung-onil, Ortho MAX, Daconil), azoxystrobin, mancozeb, myclobutanil, or thiophanate-methyl, strictly according to the label.

canonical.summary: Foliar blight causes yellowing to reddish brown discoloration of leaves and general thinning of the turf, with leaves dying from their tips down; basal rot causes scattered plants or small patches to turn yellow and die, with a water-soaked black rot of the crown tissue. On annual bluegrass putting greens, symptoms typically appear as bright yellowing of turf in irregular patterns, with patches an inch or two to more than a foot across.
diagnostic_features: The most reliable diagnostic features are the dark/black coloration at the base of the plant (crowns, roots, and lower stem bases) and the presence of fungal spore-producing structures (acervuli) on stems and leaves, which look like small pin cushions and bear protruding, black, hairlike structures (setae) observable with a hand lens.
treatments: Alleviate conditions that cause turf stress (aeration, redirecting traffic, reduced watering, and tree pruning or removal)
Adequate / light, frequent nitrogen fertilization (~3.0 lb/1,000 ft2/year) to reduce anthracnose severity on annual bluegrass putting greens, without overstimulating turf during heat stress
Do not apply nitrogen at high rates during periods of high temperature stress or drought
Fertilize with complete fertilizers, avoiding deficiencies of potassium and phosphorous; soil test to avoid potassium deficiencies
Water deeply and infrequently; irrigation at 60-80% of ET is preferred
Increase mowing height (cutting heights of 0.141 inch) and reduce mowing frequency; avoid mowing below 0.125 inch and scalping
Lightweight rolling with smooth rollers to maintain green speed
Light and frequent sand topdressing
Reduce soil compaction by core aeration in spring and fall; manage thatch
Modify traffic patterns and move cups frequently
Minimize leaf wetness by improving air circulation, watering early in the day, and/or dew removal
Wash mowers thoroughly after mowing areas where disease is active
Renovate greens with newer, less susceptible bentgrass cultivars

Preventive fungicide programs (beginning 2-4 weeks before symptoms appear) using penetrant fungicides or penetrant/contact combinations at label rates; preventive applications are more effective than curative
For basal rot, apply and water in a systemic fungicide to reach the crown, followed by a separate protectant application
Avoid Group 3 fungicides (DMIs) during the summer stress period to avoid growth regulator effects
Alternate active ingredients / fungicide classes and mix contact with penetrant fungicides to delay resistance
