diagnostic_features.value: The most reliable diagnostic features are the dark/black coloration at the base of the plant (crowns, roots, and lower stem bases) and the presence of fungal spore-producing structures (acervuli) on stems and leaves, which look like small pin cushions and bear protruding, black, hairlike structures (setae) observable with a hand lens.
diagnostic_features.quote: The distinctive fruiting bodies (acervuli) of the fungus with their protruding, black, hairlike structures (setae) can be observed with a hand lens.

treatments.value: Alleviate conditions that cause turf stress (aeration, redirecting traffic, reduced watering, and tree pruning or removal); Adequate / light, frequent nitrogen fertilization (~3.0 lb/1,000 ft2/year) to reduce anthracnose severity on annual bluegrass putting greens, without overstimulating turf during heat stress; Do not apply nitrogen at high rates during periods of high temperature stress or drought; Fertilize with complete fertilizers, avoiding deficiencies of potassium and phosphorous; soil test to avoid potassium deficiencies; Water deeply and infrequently; irrigation at 60-80% of ET is preferred; Increase mowing height (cutting heights of 0.141 inch) and reduce mowing frequency; avoid mowing below 0.125 inch and scalping; Lightweight rolling with smooth rollers to maintain green speed; Light and frequent sand topdressing; Reduce soil compaction by core aeration in spring and fall; manage thatch; Modify traffic patterns and move cups frequently; Minimize leaf wetness by improving air circulation, watering early in the day, and/or dew removal; Wash mowers thoroughly after mowing areas where disease is active; Renovate greens with newer, less susceptible bentgrass cultivars; Preventive fungicide programs (beginning 2-4 weeks before symptoms appear) using penetrant fungicides or penetrant/contact combinations at label rates; preventive applications are more effective than curative; For basal rot, apply and water in a systemic fungicide to reach the crown, followed by a separate protectant application; Avoid Group 3 fungicides (DMIs) during the summer stress period to avoid growth regulator effects; Alternate active ingredients / fungicide classes and mix contact with penetrant fungicides to delay resistance
treatments.quote: Alleviate conditions that cause turf stress. Preventive applications of fungicides are recommended where the disease is a chronic problem. Fertilize with complete fertilizers, avoiding deficiencies of potassium and phosphorous.

diagnostic_features: Presence of a pinkish to salmon mass of spores, black stroma, and black setae (bristle-like fungal structures visible with a hand lens); conidia are hyaline, nonseptate, oblong and 4-6 x 13-19 micrometers; whisker-like setae can be seen in the pink spore masses under a hand lens or microscope.

treatments: Use disease-free seed and consider seed treatments to ensure no pathogens are present
Inspect each seedling for freedom from leaf spots before taking from nursery to field; destroy seedlings with leaf spots
Do not plant near older crops of cucumber, melon, or watermelon, especially those with signs of anthracnose
Practice at least a one-year, preferably two or three-year, rotation away from cucurbit crops (leave a 2-3 year gap with no cucurbit family crops)
Avoid overhead irrigation since water splash spreads the fungus; if used, irrigate in the early morning so foliage dries before nightfall
Avoid working in or moving machinery through crops when leaves and vines are wet, since people and equipment can spread spores
Control weeds, especially wild or volunteer cucurbits
Plough in or remove crop residues in infected fields; 'flip plow' the field with a modified moldboard plow; practice fall tillage
Use resistant cultivars of watermelon and pickling/slicing cucumbers (resistant varieties are not available for melon)
Do not save seeds from fields where anthracnose has been observed
Use fungicides to prevent disease at or before the time vines begin to touch within the row; begin spraying at first appearance of disease, then every 5 to 10 days (shorter interval in rainy weather)

canonical.summary: On redcedar/juniper, dark brown swollen galls (up to two inches diameter) with circular dimples form on branches and produce bright orange gelatinous telial horns in spring. On apple/crabapple, small chlorotic yellow spots develop on leaves that turn orange with red rings, bearing orange pustules above and hairy tube-like aecia below; fruit develops yellow/orange lesions that turn brown with tube-like aecia.
diagnostic_features: Galls on juniper/redcedar always have small circular dimples across the surface, from which bright orange gelatinous telial horns (1/2 to 3/4 inch long) erupt in spring. On apple/crabapple leaves, yellow spots develop red rings around the edge, small raised black dots in the center on the upper surface, and produce hairy, finger-like aecia (less than 1/10 inch) on the leaf underside; on crabapple fruits the aecia give the fruits a spiky appearance.
treatments: Plant disease-resistant varieties of crabapple, apple, and juniper
Avoid planting eastern red cedar and juniper within several miles / a few hundred yards of susceptible Rosaceae plants
Inspect nearby juniper/red cedar trees in late winter or early spring and remove brown, woody galls before orange gelatinous structures form
Prune and remove infected twigs or branches on Rosaceae plants
Apply fungicides on the primary (juniper) host every 14 days from June to September

Apply fungicides on apple/crabapple beginning around flowering and continuing on a seven-day interval until telial horns dry up; sterol inhibitors (e.g., Myclobutanil) are most effective; copper and sulfur products can also be used
Spray trees/shrubs when flower buds first emerge until spring weather becomes consistently warm and dry
For organic apple production: bloom thinning combined with lime sulfur or a labelled biofungicide
Tolerate leaf spots and fruit infection on apples, hawthorns, serviceberry, and other Rosaceae
Avoid planting highly susceptible varieties such as Beacon and Wealthy apple where cedar-apple rust is a problem

On the pome fruits, symptoms begin as small yellow or orange lesions, which eventually grow larger and turn brown.

canonical.summary: White, powdery fungal growth develops on both leaf surfaces, petioles, and stems (primarily asexual conidia), usually first on crown leaves, shaded lower leaves and leaf undersurfaces; yellow spots may form on upper leaf surfaces opposite the colonies, infected leaves shrivel and die, and plants may senesce prematurely.
diagnostic_features: White, powdery fungal growth (conidia) on both leaf surfaces, petioles and stems, developing first on crown leaves, shaded lower leaves and leaf undersurfaces, with yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces opposite the colonies; older plants are affected first. The first sign is often pale yellow leaf spots.
treatments: Plant varieties with complete or partial resistance to powdery mildew; select varieties with resistance from both parents (homozygous resistance) when possible.
Provide good air movement around plants through proper spacing, staking, and weed control; choose planting sites free of shade.
Apply fertilizer based on soil test results and avoid over-applying nitrogen.

Inspect/scout crops routinely (particularly lower leaf surfaces) beginning at the start of crop development; the action threshold for starting applications is one leaf with symptoms out of 50 older leaves examined.
Physically separate successive cucurbit plantings (or plant up-wind of older plantings) to prevent older plants serving as an inoculum source for the main crop.
Before disease appears / early in disease development, apply fungicides on a 7 to 10-day interval following detection through an IPM scouting program.
Alternate products with different modes of action / FRAC groups to avoid generating fungicide-resistant strains, and include a protectant fungicide in every application.

Use mobile (systemic or translaminar) fungicides tank-mixed with a contact fungicide, applied only when needed at the highest labeled rates, alternating among as many different mobile fungicides as possible.
Recommended protectant fungicides include chlorothalonil, sulfur, copper, mineral oil, and several biopesticides; sulfur is one of the most effective and least expensive products.
Remove debris, weeds, and volunteers that may harbor the pathogen.
Organic growers: fixed copper formulations are the only OMRI-labeled active ingredients with some efficacy against cucurbit powdery mildew.
Home gardeners: products containing copper or chlorothalonil are the best effective products available, combined with growing tolerant varieties.

canonical.summary: Initial symptoms are yellowish or chlorotic flecks on leaves (especially those in contact with soil) that enlarge into elliptical, tan-brown lesions, often with yellowish halos. Lesion centers die, becoming bleached gray or ash-white, and produce small, dark brown to black pycnidia, giving the lesion a characteristic speckled appearance. Subsequent lesions on higher leaves generally follow leaf veins, with straight edges and no yellow margins.
diagnostic_features: The presence of small, black pycnidia in lesions is the most reliable in-field character for identifying the disease. Lesions generally do not have pronounced chlorotic halos like Stagonospora leaf and glume blotch and tan spot, and lesions are more elongated with rougher edges. When humid, a translucent, curling thread of whitish (or pinkish-brown, column-shaped, jellylike) ooze of spores (conidia) may exude from the pycnidia and is visible with a hand lens.

canonical.summary: Causes sudden wilt, death of sprouts and melt down of storage roots, with damage ranging from small tire-size dead spots to the loss of entire beds.
diagnostic_features: Characterized by the production of rapidly growing white mycelium and the yellow to brown mustard seed-like sclerotia that serve as survival structures and are produced on the mycelium.
treatments: Site selection: Choose a well-drained site for the plant bed that has not had sweetpotatoes for at least 3 to 4 years.
Plant handling: Cut plants in beds 1 inch above the soil line. Do not pull plants. Use disease-free planting stock.
Removal of bed covers: bed covers should be removed as soon as the sprouts emerge from seed roots.
Deep plowing: The sclerotia do not survive when buried at least 8 inches into soil with a breaking plow.
Solarization: the soil may be covered with black polyethylene sheets for a 6 week period during the hottest months of the year.

Chemical control: Dipping roots prior to bedding, or to a lesser extent, spraying roots laid out in beds with a protectant fungicide such as dichloran (Botran) can reduce the incidence of Southern blight.

Make in-furrow or banded applications with azoxystrobin (Quadris) shortly after transplanting. Drenching the beds with Quadris at 15.4 ounces per acre using a minimum of 35 gallons of water may provide some suppression of Southern blight in plant beds.
Soil fumigation with chloropicrin can aid in reducing inoculum and Southern blight incidence.

canonical.summary: On leaves, yellow spots or purple ring spots may appear, with feathery patterns along the veins that may be yellow or purple; in many cases there are no symptoms or they are faint and short-lived. On roots, strain RC causes external cracking in rings around the storage roots and internal cork (small brown to black corky spots).
diagnostic_features: Purple feathery-like patterns along veins typical of infection; strain RC causes external cracking in rings around storage roots and internal cork (small brown to black corky spots).

Use planting material, produced through a healthy 'seed' scheme
Remove wild Ipomoea species if they are present around the sweet potato plantings
Remove old, harvested, vines and, if possible, plant new crops away from older ones that might be a source of aphids and viruses
Use resistant varieties
Chemical control is not a method that can be used to control this virus

summary.quote: On its own, there may be yellow spots (Photo 1), or purple ring spots (Photo 2). Feathery patterns may appear along the veins, and these too may be yellow or purple (Photos 3&4). In many cases, there are no symptoms, or they are faint and short-lived, with the new leaves looking healthy. On the roots, the symptoms, depend on the strain and the variety. Strain O does not produce symptoms, whereas strain RC causes external cracking in rings around the storage roots (Photo 5), and internal cork – small brown to black corky spots, seen after harvest and during storage.

canonical.summary: Greenish-gray water-soaked lesions appear on the leaf sheath near the water level, circular to oblong or ellipsoid and about 1 cm long. Lesions enlarge to irregular shape with gray-white centers and brown margins, and can spread to upper sheaths, leaf blades and panicles causing rotting, leaf drying and seed discoloration.
diagnostic_features: Greenish-gray water-soaked lesions on the leaf sheath near the water level, circular/oblong/ellipsoid ~1 cm long, enlarging with gray-white centers and brown margins; at field level the infection affects plants in a circular pattern referred to as 'bird's nest'.
treatments: Use resistant rice varieties / develop resistant genotypes

Use a reasonable level of fertilizer adapted to the cropping season; apply balanced K, Zn, S, Fe; use slow-release nitrogenous fertilizer (e.g., Crotonylidene diurea, Guanyl urea phosphate) with silica, phosphorus and potash
Use reasoned density of crop establishment (direct seeding or transplanting); improve canopy architecture by reducing seeding rate or providing wider plant spacing
Carefully control weeds, especially on the levees
Drain rice fields relatively early in the cropping season to reduce sheath blight epidemics
Use fungicide to treat seeds; apply chemical fungicides as needed
Apply soil amendments including neem cake, farm yard manure (FYM), vermicompost and rice husk
Spray Ganoderma diethyl ester biological formulation
Use resistance-linked molecular markers in breeding programs; use non-host plants as a genetic resource for developing resistant rice varieties
Use novel biotechnological approaches such as RNAi, transgenics and genome-editing (e.g., transgenic rice overexpressing oxalate oxidase)

diagnostic_features: Black lesions on the root surface with a well-defined border between infected and healthy tissues that may not penetrate deeply and enlarge slowly even near freezing; dry, mealy, black storage decay; blackened hypocotyls and deformed roots; petiole lesions extending to the vascular system causing yellowing, wilting, and plant death.
treatments: Use pathogen-free seed and, for seed crops, obtain transplant carrots free of Alternaria infection
Eradicate A. radicina from seed with a hot water treatment (122Â°F for 30 min)
Rotate out of carrots for at least 1 year (3-4 years recommended) since refuse is the main overwintering route
Plow under / promptly incorporate crop debris soon after harvest
Irrigate so that carrots are dry by nightfall
Plant tolerant cultivars (e.g. Improved Half Long Chantenay, K-2043)
Control storage rot by washing, culling, minimizing wounding/breakage, and storing at 0-1Â°C

canonical.summary: Symptoms include marginal yellowing and browning of leaves beginning with the lower leaves, progressing to entire discoloration, wilting, and collapse, with rotted petiole bases and mushy crowns; a white mat of fungus and tiny spherical sclerotia appear at the crown and soil surface.
diagnostic_features: Because the bases of the petioles are rotted, the leaves can be easily pulled away from the crown; a white mat of fungus (mycelium) fans out from the infected crown across the soil surface, and thousands of tiny, spherical sclerotia (BB to pepper grounds in size, white to brick red) are present in the rotted crown.
look_alikes: Other basal stem rots such as those caused by Rhizoctonia or other fungi
treatments: Dig up/dig and burn or remove hostas showing crown rot symptoms.
Thoroughly scrape and/or wash soil from all tools used in infested soil, then sterilize tools in a 10% solution of household bleach.
Buy disease-free plants / use only pathogen free stock.
Plant nonhost species into holes from which sick hostas have been excavated.
Follow good Integrated Pest Management practices to avoid fungicide applications.
Solarize or otherwise pasteurize soil before planting.
Remove soil from affected area and replace with new or sterilized soil.
Avoid overwatering and provide good soil drainage, for example, by planting in raised beds.
Rhizomes or bulbs can be treated with hot water to eliminate the fungus.
Soil drenches of fungicides (Cleary's 3336, Terraclor) around the base of plants before infection can prevent disease development (but will not cure affected plants).
Amendment of the soil with biological control agents such as MycoStop, PlantShield, SoilGard, or YieldShield may offer some control.

canonical.summary: Disease often begins as tiny, almost translucent spots that turn brown and water-soaked; infected fruit, leaves, petals, and succulent stems become dark, soft, and wilted and die. On flowers, water-soaked petal spots develop reddish-brown blotches and buds may die before opening. Under high humidity a thin to thick grayish web of mycelium develops on diseased tissue, hence the name gray mold.
diagnostic_features: A fuzz of grayish-brown fungal sporulation (a thin to thick grayish web of mycelium) develops on dead/diseased tissue under humid conditions, giving rotted tissue a fuzzy or woolly appearance. When inner or middle petals develop brown lesions first, gray mold is the likely cause; on thin leaves (e.g. redbud) lesions are light brown to brown and irregular, while on fleshier leaves (e.g. rhododendron) concentric rings of different shades of brown may be visible.
treatments: Control the environment and keep plants healthy by avoiding stresses such as plants staying too wet or too dry, chemical or mechanical injury, and too little or too much fertilizer.
Improve air circulation and sunlight; adequately space plants and prune canopies, and cut back nearby and overhead vegetation.
Avoid overhead or late-evening watering; use drip or microsprinkler irrigation and avoid wetting foliage.
Especially keep open flowers with many petals dry.
Maintain low humidity in the greenhouse and avoid sunburn by planting in shadier locations.
Avoid wounding leaves or shoots.

Use good sanitation: dead-head dying flowers, remove and dispose of old blossoms, infected plant tissue, crop debris (especially spent blooms), fallen leaves, and weeds; do not practice sanitation when plants are wet.
Destroy infected tissue by burning where permitted, or bury it under at least a foot of soil.
Apply fungicides to help prevent or reduce leaf, fruit, and stem infections; chlorothalonil, thiophanate-methyl, or triforine can be applied before disease develops.
Tank-mix and/or alternate products from different groups with different modes of action to prevent buildup of resistant fungi.

Labeled chemical products include Astun (Group 7), Bonide Fung-onil Multi-purpose Fungicide, Broadform (Group 7+11), Chipco 26019 FLO (Group 2), Daconil Weather Stik (Group M5), Decree 50 WDG (Group 17), mancozeb-based Fore 80WP/Protect DF (Group M3), OHP 6672 4.5 F (Group 1), Orkestra (Group 7+11), Pageant (Group 7+11), Palladium (Group 9+12), Phyton 27 (Group M1), Postiva (Group 3+7), Spectro 90 WDG (Group 1+M5), and Terraguard SC (Group 3).
Biological control: BotryStop (Ulocladium oudemansii U3 strain) at 2 to 4 lb/A, kept refrigerated before use.

Use adequate plant spacing and good weed control to encourage air movement.
Remove infected plants from the area and do not compost.
Try to harvest mature plants with a minimum of injury.
Properly cure garlic bulbs with good air movement; if normal dry weather prevails, cure garlic on the ground for 6 to 10 days.
Practice proper crop rotation.
Do not plant garlic or other alliums in a field where the pathogen is present.
Allow the tops to mature well, then lift or undercut the garlic.
When topping, keep bruising and mechanical injury to a minimum.

diagnostic_features: Waxy, yellow-orange pustules containing masses of spores form on one year old needles and erupt at bud break to release yellow-orange spores; after sporulation needles may become rusty brown and drop during the summer, with severity often highest on lower canopy branches.
treatments: Fungicide application to newly developing needles shortly after budbreak can suppress new infections

Removing infected one year old needles to reduce inoculum in late winter or early spring prior to the release of spores

Use seed that does not have significant levels of the pathogen.

Avoid overhead irrigation and dense plant canopies.
Protectant fungicides are recommended for control.
To be effective, fungicides must be applied before fruit formation.

canonical.summary: Symptoms are characterized by dark-colored, irregularly-shaped, angular spots or blotches that occur primarily along the midrib, primary veins and leaf margins; they appear in late spring or summer as scattered, sharply defined reddish-brown dead areas on or near leaf veins, may enlarge and coalesce to kill large areas of leaves, cause twisting/crinkling/malformation, and severely diseased trees can defoliate early.
diagnostic_features: Lesions occur primarily along the midrib, primary veins and leaf margins (narrow, purplish-black streaks on Norway maple; large brown blotches on sugar maple; tan or black lesions on Japanese maple); acervuli (spore pads) form within leaf spots and blotches. A. apocryptum is distinguished from other maple pathogens by its formation of one-celled, colorless conidia in groups of four to eight on the tips of short, broad conidiophores.

Prune trees to remove and destroy dead or diseased wood, including shoots infected with fire blight, and burn it to reduce inoculum
Chopping/flail-mowing dead wood on the ground to remove bark and increase decomposition
Remove and burn (eliminate) mummified fruit from trees and the orchard floor throughout the growing season
Maintain tree vigor with a balanced fertility program (based on soil/foliar analyses), proper watering, and annual pruning
Do not use susceptible cultivars; select resistant cultivars and prune canopies open and well-ventilated to reduce surface wetness
Apply fungicides from fruit set / first cover until harvest where a good sanitation program is in place

canonical.summary: On Eastern white pine, needles on infected branches turn yellow then rusty red, and branches develop swollen cankers with discolored, cracked bark that ooze sticky sap and form white-to-yellow blisters releasing orange spores. On Ribes plants (currant and gooseberry), angular yellow leaf spots appear on the upper leaf surface with raised orange pustules on the underside.
diagnostic_features: On pine: cankers on the main trunk are oval or diamond-shaped, often with a dead branch in the center, oozing sticky clear-to-white sap, with white-to-yellow blisters releasing powdery orange spores and gummy orange spore droplets. On Ribes: angular yellow leaf spots contained by leaf veins with raised orange pustules and orange or brown hair-like tendrils on the leaf underside.
treatments: Diseased pine branches should be pruned out of the tree before the infection comes within 4 inches of the main trunk.
Prune off branches with cankers at a branch union or where the branch meets the trunk. Remove at least 4 inches of healthy wood beyond the visible symptoms of disease.
Remove lower branches gradually as the trees mature; never remove more than 1/3 of the canopy at a time.
When planting white pine trees, space plants to promote good air movement around the trees. Redirect lawn sprinklers or irrigation systems to avoid wetting pine needles.
Don't plant eastern white pine and currants or gooseberry together in the landscape unless resistant cultivars are used. Avoid planting white pine in low lying areas or cold pockets.
Plant resistant varieties â€” 'Paton's Silver Splendor' eastern white pine and resistant gooseberry and currant cultivars are available.
Eradicating Ribes plants has not worked to eliminate the disease but may help slow the disease spread.

Pruning off the lower branches can help if done before rust symptoms on the branches get within six inches of the trunk; pruned branches can be left since the pathogen cannot survive in dried out tissue.
If symptoms develop within six inches of the trunk, removal of the tree is suggested to help reduce spread of disease.

canonical.summary: Aspens develop vivid orange bark patches ranging from fluorescent orange to wet, oozing orange-black; cankers appear as sunken, discolored zones that girdle branches or stems and cause dieback.
diagnostic_features: Cankers first appear as sunken, discolored zones with raised edges or bright orange patches; the inner bark progressively changes from bright orange to black and can have a foul odor; after 2 to 3 years the dead bark falls off in large pieces, and sapwood is stained light to reddish-brown. Under moist conditions, masses of spores ooze out of pimple-like pycnidia in long, orange, coiled, thread-like spore tendrils.
treatments: Remove all dead and dying branches on affected trees, and remove and destroy (burn or bury) dead or severely cankered branches
If cankers are confined to twigs or branches, cut diseased bark and discolored wood back 1 to 2 inches into surrounding live, healthy tissue with a sharp knife; avoid leaving branch stubs
Do not prune or work around trees when the bark is wet, and prune or cut trees only during dry weather
Sterilize pruning tools between cuts (70 percent rubbing alcohol, ethyl alcohol, Lysol, or bleach/Clorox at 1 part to 9 parts water)
Severely cankered trees should be cut down and burned; stands with a high proportion of cankered stems should be clearcut to stimulate sucker regeneration

Reduce stress and keep trees in good vigor: prepare soil, fertilize, water properly for winter and summer, use resistant/site-adapted species, purchase healthy nursery stock, and avoid wounding the trunk and limbs
Clean wounds and remove dead bark to dry out the diseased area; do not apply tar, oil-based paint, or other wound dressing
Control insects to prevent combined stress; on peach and cherry, apply labeled fungicides as wound dressings at pruning wounds
Conifer control to reduce moisture stress and increase sunlight (without injuring aspen), and minimize livestock browsing with fencing or conifer slash

canonical.summary: Small, bleached light-brown to tan spots appear first on the upper surface of one-year-old leaves; one or several brown to black fruiting structures (apothecia) form in the center of the spots in late spring; leaves turn brown and drop in fall, while infected leaves remaining on the tree turn ashy gray.
diagnostic_features: Apothecia are embedded in the leaf tissues and the entire structure drops out, leaving deep pits; the disease progression gives the appearance of having been scorched by fire.
treatments: Application of fungicides to manage the disease is rarely necessary
A copper fungicide (Bordeaux Mix) or mancozeb (Dithane) should be effective if applied early in the season, when susceptible foliage is developing
Propagate from disease-free stock plants
Use seed from British Columbia coastal, low-elevation populations
Space nursery plants and time irrigation to promote rapid drying of foliage
Do not grow susceptible cultivars downwind of infected hedges, windbreaks, or nearby stands of native western red cedar
Pruning out and burning affected twigs is of limited use
Remove plant debris from seed before seeding
Apply fungicides during wet periods in spring and fall to protect healthy foliage
Banner MAXX at 5 to 8 fl oz/100 gal water can be used if not phytotoxic to plants
Topas (propiconazole) registered in British Columbia for use every 4 weeks during the growing season to a maximum of six applications (Group 3 fungicide, 12-hr reentry)
Bordeaux or fixed-copper sprays (such as CuPRO 5000 at 1.5 to 2 lb/A) in spring and early summer (48-hr reentry)
Mancozeb-based products applied as regular sprays late March through May and late August through October (Group M3, 24-hr reentry)
Tebuject 16 registered for tree injections, number of capsules based on tree size

canonical.summary: Foliar symptoms range from angular-shaped leaf spots and blotches, marginal leaf scorch, and a complete blight of infected foliage; leaf spots are round to blotchy with tan centers and reddish-purple margins. Leaf dieback first occurs in the lower crown and works up the tree. Infection moves from leaves to twigs, where cankers develop causing twig dieback, and succulent shoots and small stems can be killed while perennial cankers develop on larger branches.
diagnostic_features: Tan leaf spots with distinctive purple borders; dead twigs appear tan and are often covered with black, pin-point fruiting bodies (conidiomata) that produce masses of orange spores in wet weather; the leaf blotch often spreads down the midvein giving a wedge-shaped appearance; vascular cambium infected with the disease is chocolate brown in contrast to the pale tan color of healthy sapwood; and prolific epicormic/water sprouts develop on the trunk and adjacent to large branch cankers.
treatments: Plant resistant species/cultivars: Cornus kousa (e.g. Milky Way, Steeple) is tolerant; C. kousa x C. florida hybrids (Celestial, StarDust, Stellar Pink, and several 'stellar' crosses) and disease-resistant C. florida cultivars greatly reduce the need for management
Practice early detection; trees with extensive dieback and only a few active branches cannot be saved and should be removed
Trees showing only initial signs (leaf spots and twig canker) can be pruned and treated with fungicides
Prune out and destroy infected/blighted twigs, shoots, and stems as they develop, and remove epicormic/water sprouts that form
Rake and remove fallen leaves from spring through fall, and remove dead twigs and leaves remaining attached to the tree
Plant in full sun with good air circulation, in well-ventilated areas where plants dry quickly after wetting, with no surrounding plantings
Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers that produce lush succulent shoots more susceptible to the fungus
Do not let irrigation wet the tree canopy; provide a soaking root-zone irrigation during droughts and maintain a 2-3 inch layer of composted mulch over the root zone
Limit additional stresses such as string trimmer and mower damage

Apply protective fungicide sprays beginning at bud break/budbreak, repeating every 10-14 days until leaves are fully open / until dry weather, with an additional application in late summer when flower buds form
Alternate or tank-mix fungicide products from different groups (modes of action) to prevent resistance; limit use of any one group during the growing season

canonical.summary: First symptoms are small, chlorotic to yellow spots; spots on the upper leaf surface turn reddish-brown and leaves may die if spots coalesce and become necrotic. On the leaf underside, yellowish-orange pustules (uredinia) develop that turn rusty-red with age, and infected leaves usually drop prematurely.
diagnostic_features: Dusty clumps of yellow-, orange-, or rust-colored spores (urediniospores) on the underside of the leaf, opposite the upper leaf lesions; when present these spores distinguish leaf rust from all other leaf spot diseases. Lesions can be limited by larger leaf veins, resulting in lesions with parallel straight or angular sides.
treatments: Integrate horticultural and chemical methods to reduce the impact of the disease.
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead irrigation where and whenever possible.
When overhead irrigation is necessary, time the application to avoid extended periods of leaf wetness and to occur after dew formation in early morning hours.
Plant spacing, maintenance pruning to increase airflow in the canopy, and controlling weeds in row middles.
Remove hemlocks upwind from where blueberry is grown.
Grow less susceptible cultivars.
Prompt removal and disposal of fallen leaves may be helpful.
Make repeated fungicide applications to maintain a protective residue on the leaves; scout during post-bloom and early fall periods.
Chemical control: start when leaves first begin to break bud and unfold; continue at regular intervals during wet weather.
chlorothalonil (e.g., Bravo TM / Bravo Weather Stik, Group M5; after harvest only) applications for rust management can begin late fall, before bloom.
Proline TM / Proline 480 SC (prothioconazole), an excellent DMI choice for rust (seven-day PHI).
Quilt Xcel TM / QuiltXcel (azoxystrobin and propiconazole, Group 3 + 11).
Propulse TM (fluopyram and prothioconazole, Group 3 + 7).
Other DMIs with longer preharvest intervals if rust increases before bloom (e.g., Indar TM, Tilt TM).
Quash TM for flare-ups closer to harvest.
Quadris Flowable / Quadris Top and Pristine TM have rust efficacy and make good rotation partners with a DMI product.
Consider tank mixing a captan product with Quadris Flowable or Pristine TM.
Bordeaux 8-8-100 plus spreader-sticker; copper products (e.g., Kocide 50 DF, Nu-Cop 50 DF) â€” not for use in the spring.
Inspire Super (Group 3 + 9).
Regalia (Group P5) â€” may be used day of harvest.
Organic management options include copper products and plant-based horticultural oils.
Biological control: Sonata (Bacillus pumilis strain QST 2808) plus a spreader-sticker; may be applied up to and including the day of harvest.
Fungicides with different modes of action should be used in rotation or in a tank mix as part of an integrated postharvest foliage management strategy.

canonical.summary: Signs and symptoms include white woolly scale insects on the bark, orange cankers with rough callous edges that may exude a red-brown fluid, and small bright red fungal fruiting bodies (perithecia) on the bark in fall; severe infection causes girdling, stem breakage, and death.
diagnostic_features: Adult beech scale insects are round, soft-bodied, and yellow, often noticed due to the white, woolly substance they create; cankers may appear orange with rough edges and may exude a red-brown fluid; fungal perithecia are small and bright red, produced in clusters as superficial perithecia (each about 0.25 mm diameter), while irregular, blocky bark indicates a host resistance response.
treatments: Insecticides may be used to prevent infection, more effective if timed for the crawler stage before it develops a protective waxy covering
Scale insects may be mechanically removed from landscape trees
Care for landscape trees properly to improve overall tree health
Promote and breed/plant resistant beech trees in forests
Report suspected cases of BBD to the North Carolina Forest Service - Forest Health Branch
Silvicultural selective harvesting of larger beech (about 45% basal area reduction) to improve overstory growth of sugar maple and birch

summary.quote: Scale insects ( Fig. 1 ), cankers ( Fig 2 , 3 ), and fungal fruiting bodies ( Fig. 4 ) are some signs and symptoms of BBD.

diagnostic_features.quote: These cankers may appear orange, and edges of the cankers become rough as the tree creates callous tissue. Cankers may also exude a red-brown fluid which seeps down the bark . Further, fruiting bodies (perithecia) of the fungi are often present on bark in the fall. These perithecia are small and bright red in color.

treatments.quote: Since BBD begins with feeding by the beech scale insect, insecticides may be used to prevent infection. These insecticides are more effective if timed for the crawler stage because this stage does not yet have a protective waxy covering. Scale insects may also be mechanically removed from landscape trees.

affected_parts.quote: Upon settling, beech scales use their specialized mouthparts to penetrate the bark and suck sap from the phloem of beech trees. As this occurs, areas of the tree become damaged, creating fissures.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: There are two species of Neonectria fungi that contribute to BBD: the native N. galligena and the non-native N. faginata (sometimes referred to as N. coccinea var. faginata).

type_of_disease.quote: a combination of feeding damage by a scale insect and cankers caused by a fungal pathogen

canonical.summary: Individual buds turn brown and die, followed by browning and necrosis of bark around the bud as the fungus spreads into the twig, causing dieback of fruit-bearing twigs.
diagnostic_features: The disease stops progressing after killing the twig (6-10 inches) and does not progress further down the stem to infect older wood; pycnidia are evident in diseased tissues.
treatments: Pruning can be performed to remove infected twigs prior to spore release in the spring
Commercial growers who mow bushes in June and July after harvest (topping) will also benefit from the removal of blighted twigs
Careful cultivar selection can greatly reduce the amount of twig blight experienced; newer cultivars (Legacy, New Hanover, O'Neal, Star, Farthing) are generally resistant to twig blight
Chemical control can be achieved by spraying labeled fungicides from budbreak through bloom on a 7-14 day interval

canonical.summary: Infected woody plants show thinning canopies, browning and prematurely shedding foliage, scattered branch dieback, and eruptive cankers on the bark, sometimes with sunken sap-stained lesions and oozing sap; in many cases the only symptoms are leaf wilting and canopy dieback.
diagnostic_features: After establishing in the canopy, the pathogen produces an abundance of small, black-colored pads of fungal tissue (pycnidia) that erupt through the bark to release cream-colored spore tendrils (cirrhi).
treatments: Minimize stresses that predispose woody plants to infection and maintain high plant vigor
Irrigate susceptible trees and shrubs at regular intervals during extended dry periods to minimize drought stress
Fertilize if soil nutrients are lacking and mulch the root zone to retain soil moisture
Limit mechanical wounds (e.g. string trimmers) and avoid needless damage to canopy and roots
Avoid excessive pruning, especially on recently transplanted plants, and avoid pruning during wet spring periods
Perform regular sanitation pruning to remove dead twigs; prune cankered stems/branches at least 6-12 inches away from blighted tissue and remove diseased material from the site
Sanitize pruning tools after working with infected or suspected plants

Apply registered fungicides in spring to protect newly developing tissues (azoxystrobin, captan, copper salts of fatty and rosin acids, copper hydroxide, mancozeb, metconazole, phosphites, propiconazole, tebuconazole, thiophanate-methyl); avoid application on actively flowering plants to protect pollinators

summary.quote: Typical symptoms of infection include thinning canopies, browning and prematurely shedding foliage, scattered branch dieback, and eruptive cankers on the bark. There may also be sunken lesions on shoots and branches with sap-stained bark, along with cracking, splitting, and sloughing bark or oozing sap near the canker site (Sinclair and Lyon 2005).

treatments.quote: Pruning of cankered stems and branches, at least 6-12 inches away from the blighted tissue (if possible), and removal of the diseased material from the site is the best management practice. ... Fungicides registered for use against Phomopsis include: azoxystrobin captan, copper salts of fatty and rosin acids, copper hydroxide, mancozeb, metconazole, phosphites, propiconazole, tebuconazole, and thiophanate-methyl.

affected_parts.quote: Phomopsis can cause cankers of young shoots, small stems and branches, and occasionally primary branches and the main trunk of trees and shrubs (Sinclair and Lyon 2005).

type_of_disease.quote: Cankering fungi like Phomopsis attack the phloem, cambium, and outer sapwood of woody plants (Sinclair and Lyon 2005).

canonical.summary: Phyllosticta-infected arborvitae show blighted needle tips and pale green to yellow, desiccated-looking needles, with infections progressing from tip toward the base; Pestalotiopsis causes browning and dieback that can kill small branches.
diagnostic_features: During wet, mild weather black pads of fungal tissue (pycnidia) rupture through the needle epidermis to release spores; Pestalotiopsis produces small pads under the epidermis that rupture to form a long black mass of spores and attacks stems and small branches, whereas Phyllosticta is primarily restricted to the needles.
treatments: Prune and discard as many infected plant parts as possible
Avoid pruning during wet weather, when the fungus is most actively producing and disseminating spores
Avoid watering with overhead sprinklers that wet the foliage
Use drip irrigation or hand-watering of newly planted trees
Apply fungicides labeled for use on ornamentals (copper hydroxide, copper salts of fatty and rosin acids, metconazole, propiconazole, thiophanate-methyl and mancozeb)
Use fungicides preventatively to limit infections on the current year's growth in the spring
Use proper spacing and planting techniques to alleviate predisposing stresses

canonical.summary: White, powdery fungal growth develops on both leaf surfaces, petioles, and stems, usually developing first on crown leaves, shaded lower leaves, and leaf undersurfaces; affected leaves senesce early and fruit yield and quality can be reduced.
diagnostic_features: Yellow spots may form on upper leaf surfaces opposite the powdery mildew colonies; older plants are affected first; late in the season dark brown, very small (about 0.003 inches) chasmothecia that are barely discernable without a hand lens may develop.
treatments: Manage with resistant varieties/cultivars; an integrated program using both resistant varieties and fungicides is the best approach for effective control
Apply fungicides on a 7 to 10-day interval beginning very early in disease development (before disease appears / following IPM-based detection)
Initiate a weekly spray program when symptoms are found; action threshold is one leaf with symptoms out of 50 older leaves examined
Alternate products with different modes of action / FRAC groups and include a protectant fungicide in every application to manage fungicide resistance
Apply mobile (systemic) fungicides together with a contact/protectant fungicide as a tank mix, at highest labeled rates, only when needed to protect yield
Provide adequate plant spacing; choose planting sites with good air movement and free of shade
Physically separate successive cucurbit plantings or plant up-wind of older plantings, which can serve as a source of conidia
Remove debris, weeds, and volunteers that may harbor the pathogen
Scout fields regularly, particularly lower leaf surfaces, beginning at the start of crop development

Example conventional products: Chlorothalonil (Bravo Weather Stik), Myclobutanil (Rally 40WSP), Pyraclostrobin + boscalid (Pristine), Quinoxyfen (Quintec), Metrafenone (Vivando), Cyflufenamid (Torino), Azoxystrobin + difenoconazole (Quadris Top)
Organic growers: fixed copper formulations are the only OMRI-labeled active ingredients with some efficacy; several biopesticides approved for organic production are registered
Home gardeners: products containing copper or chlorothalonil (e.g., 'Daconil') are the best effective options; also grow tolerant varieties

canonical.summary: Symptoms include bleeding of color out from the leaf veins, blue or dark green mottling on the leaves, leaf distortion (puckering and twisting), ring spots, flecks, zipper marks, stunted growth, and occasionally necrotic lesions.
diagnostic_features: Bleeding of color out from the veins of the leaves and blue or dark green mottling, along with zipper marks, ring spots, and flecks; symptoms are easier to distinguish in gold-colored cultivars, and holding an infected leaf up to the light versus a healthy leaf aids identification.
treatments: Carefully inspect any plants for color bleeding and leaf mottling before purchasing; avoid buying plants with symptoms of HVX.
When purchasing hostas (especially expensive ones), consider requesting that the seller provide proof that the plants are HVX-free.
Send samples to a diagnostic lab when HVX is suspected; virus testing kits are available and relatively inexpensive.
Before planting new plants, isolate them from any other hostas for at least 1 week (up to several weeks) and watch for symptom development.
Remove and destroy all plants that test positive or show symptoms â€” burn (where allowed) or landfill/throw away in their own trash bags. Do NOT compost.
Disinfest tools that may have contacted infected plants; for home gardeners, thoroughly scrubbing tools in hot soapy water is generally sufficient.

Professionals may use disinfectants such as Zerotol, KleenGrow, Physan, or Virkon after removing all organic matter from tools; or treat items for at least one minute with Alconox plus SLS/SDS, or trisodium phosphate solution.
Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water (for at least one minute) before and after working with the plants.
Minimize wounding that could release sap and provide an entry point for HVX.
Note: normal sterilization with 70% rubbing alcohol is NOT effective for HVX management.

canonical.summary: Symptoms include yellowing of leaf margins (chlorosis), light- to dark-brown necrotic spots on cotyledons, water-soaked stem tissue, stem lesions that girdle the stem, cracking with gummy ooze, red/brown/black cankers exuding red to amber gummy substance, and brownish-black depressed fruit lesions (black rot).
diagnostic_features: Black fruiting bodies of the fungus (pycnidia, perithecia, or pseudothecia) on infected leaves, stems, and fruits; pycnidia swell and release tendrils of spores when wetted, observable with a hand lens or microscope; large brown irregularly shaped lesions with concentric ring pattern on leaf margins and interveinal areas; stem lesions often exude a gummy, reddish-brown liquid.
treatments: Purchase seeds from reputable companies with a good history of GSB-free seed production
Seed treatment is necessary if not previously treated, and disinfectants as solutions are more effective than dry-dust treatments
Regularly inspect transplant seedlings in the greenhouses; avoid using healthy-looking seedlings from trays with infected plants
Decaying debris from that crop should be disked and deep plowed into the soil if it is to be followed by a long-term crop rotation practice
Wild citrons, balsam pear, or volunteer cucurbits are other sources of inoculum and should be eradicated before planting cucurbits
A two- to three-year rotation with non-hosts is an effective way to reduce incidence of GSB
Routine scouting of the fields helps in timely application of fungicides that can prevent major crop losses
Apply fungicides in a preventative manner. Chlorothalonil and Mancozeb are effective contact fungicides, and there are many effective systemic fungicides for management of GSB
To prevent development of fungicide resistance, various chemistries should be alternated during the spray program
Avoid wounding fruits during harvest, and store fruits at 45°F–50°F to prevent postharvest black rot
Chlorothalonil mixed with another product such as prothioconazole or tebuconazole
Mixing chlorothalonil with Luna Experience (tebuconazole and fluopyram)

canonical.summary: A pronounced bulge of callus develops around the infected area on the trunk or branch of red, sugar, silver, Norway and other maples; dead bark remains attached to the canker (which may be on one side of the trunk or completely girdle the tree), often with a dead branch stub in the center of the swollen, cankered area.
diagnostic_features: When bark is removed at the junction of diseased and healthy wood, a light tan to cream-colored mat of fungus is observed; black fungal fruiting structures protrude from the bark near the centers of 5-year-old or older cankers. The canker is usually within 10 to 12 feet of the ground with a branch stub in the center.
treatments: Remove trees with cankers on the main trunk
Remove all cankered branches, cutting 4â€“6 inches below the canker, pruning when the weather is dry

When planning to remove lower limbs, do so when they are less than 1 inch in diameter
When a limb breaks, remove the remains with a clean cut close to the branch collar without damaging the collar

treatments: Do not plant watermelon where drainage is poor, surface water accumulates, or soil is droughty.
Use a soil test to determine if there is a calcium shortage. If so, add lime, preferably in fall, to adjust soil pH to 6.8 to 7. Mix lime thoroughly in top 8 to 12 inches of soil.
Mulch plants with black plastic or loose organic material to help maintain more even soil moisture levels.
Ensure uniform soil moisture. Wet all soil in the root zone at least every 7 to 10 days. About 24 hours after watering, dig a small hole one foot deep to be certain that water penetrated that far.
Home gardeners should provide even moisture levels throughout the fruiting period if possible by controlled watering and mulching.

Ensure good air movement by plant spacing and pruning practices. By reducing relative humidity, plant transpiration increases, aiding in the uptake of calcium when sufficient amounts are present in soil.
Fertilize only moderately to keep plants normally green and vigorous but not luxuriant. Side-dress with nitrogen fertilizer only if required to maintain green color and moderate growth.

Foliar applications of calcium nitrate fertilizers or calcium chloride dihydrate (1.5 teaspoons per gal water plus 0.5 teaspoon of a surfactant such as CapSil) on a weekly basis during fruiting can provide necessary calcium to developing fruit when needed.
Making applications in early morning can help avoid spray injury.
Application of lime to fields known to be low in calcium; soil should be limed according to recommendations of soil analysis report, usually to pH 6.5-6.8.
Use of gypsum (land plaster), at rates of 500 to 1000 pounds per acre (1 to 2 pounds per 100 square feet) as a supplement to liming on calcium deficient soils.
Lime and/or gypsum should be applied several months in advance of planting.
Spraying foliage and stems with anhydrous calcium chloride (4 pounds per 100 gallons of water per acre) four times on a weekly schedule beginning when the second forms, or when symptoms first appear.
Regulate moisture supply in the soil.
Cultivation and hoeing can be avoided if proper weed-control chemicals are used. If cultivation is necessary, it should be shallow to avoid root pruning.
Irrigation supplied via a drip system.
Plants need at least one inch of water per week in the form of rain or supplemental irrigation.
Young plants should not be grown too quickly nor should the plants be subjected to severe "hardening-off" before transplanting.
Removing affected fruits when symptoms are first observed.

canonical.summary: Water-soaked oily areas with yellow halos on the underside of cotyledons or seedling leaves (often paralleling veins) that dry up into dark angular necrotic patches; small dark angled lesions on mature leaves, most often near the midrib; and a diagnostic dark green stain or blotch on the upper surface of developing fruit that rapidly expands within a week to cover the entire fruit surface and causes the rind to crack/rupture.
diagnostic_features: The diagnostic symptom is a dark green stain or blotch on the upper surface of the developing fruit, initially about 0.5 inch in diameter, rapidly expanding to cover the entire fruit surface within a week under favorable conditions; a single infected plant in a tray can infect many nearby plants resulting in a circular pattern of infection; lesions are most often near the leaf midrib; cracks in the rind develop with time.
look_alikes: Other less harmful bacteria producing identical symptoms on seedling plants
treatments: Practice good greenhouse sanitation: use a 10 percent bleach solution or Physan 20 to dip all tools, recycled planting trays, and containers for at least 10 minutes; spray benches and interior with the same solution
Thoroughly clean the greenhouse and treat with a disinfectant before each planting
Remove weeds growing in the greenhouse
Plant only tested bacteria-free seed (negative in a seedling grow-out test for BFB) from fields where no fruit blotch has been found before
Water plants evenly in early morning or by afternoon; bottom watering of transplants will help control BFB
Separate trays by lots to prevent bacterial movement between lots; segregate triploid seedless varieties and seed lots from diploid seeded varieties in the greenhouse
Reduce physical contact with seedlings; rogue diseased plants without touching healthy plants
Monitor transplants for symptoms; if suspicious symptoms are observed, remove infected plants and have them diagnosed immediately
If transplants are confirmed to have BFB, destroy all transplants from that seed lot; a greenhouse with infected transplants can be decontaminated and planted the following season
Do not transplant infected plants

In the field: rotate out of cucurbits at least every other year (2 out of every 3 years); if BFB has occurred, follow a strict three-year rotation, deep plow after harvest and control all volunteer melons and cucurbit weeds
Do not irrigate from overhead; use drip tube and plastic mulch
Fields should not be cultivated or sprayed when the foliage is wet

Begin copper spray applications if infected/suspect plants have been transplanted; apply copper hydroxide immediately after planting on a 7- to 10-day schedule if symptoms observed, or when first male flowers appear if no symptoms but BFB suspected; continue until all fruit reach maturity
Copper treatments (FRAC Group M1): Kocide 2000 / 2000-O / 3000-O, Kocide 4.5 LF, Kocide DF, Nu-Cop 50 DF, Nu-Cop 3L (copper hydroxide formulations at labeled rates)
ManKocide DF (copper hydroxide + mancozeb) at 2.5 pounds, applied at 14-day intervals; spray solution pH must be above 6.5
Badge SC at 0.5 to 2.5 pints/A on 5- to 7-day intervals
Champ Formula 2 Flowable at 0.66 to 1.33 pints/A
C-O-C-S WDG at 1 to 2 lb/A
Cuprofix Ultra 40 Disperss at 1.25 to 2 lb/A on 5- to 7-day intervals
Previsto at 0.75 to 2 quarts/A on 5- to 7-day intervals
Bonide Liquid Copper is available for home gardens

diagnostic_features: Cut a wilted vine close to the crown, press the cross-sections together, then slowly pull them apart: thread-like strands of sticky bacterial ooze form between the two cut sections, which is diagnostic (works best for cucumbers and melon, less well for squash and pumpkins).

treatments: Bacterial wilt cannot be controlled once a plant is infected; immediately remove infected plants and dispose of them by burning (where allowed by law) or burying them
DO NOT compost infected plants
If disease appears in a few plants, rogue and bury these plants to prevent further spread
Managing cucumber beetles is the most effective way to prevent bacterial wilt; remove wilted plants to keep beetles from moving bacteria to other cucurbits
Target non-chemical and chemical control of cucumber beetles at the beginning of the season when plants are most attractive to beetles
Use mechanical barriers such as floating row covers placed as seedlings emerge, removing them as flowers appear to allow pollination
In hoop houses/greenhouses, use insect exclusion screens (0.8 x 1.0 mm) to keep beetles out while allowing ventilation
Inspect cucurbits regularly for cucumber beetles and their damage (two to three times per week early, then weekly)
When cucumber beetle numbers are high (more than 20 per plant), spray with an appropriate insecticide
Use trap crops such as blue hubbard squash to reduce feeding on the main crop
Remove or destroy crop residue to reduce overwintering sites for cucumber beetles
Surround (kaolin clay) can reduce beetle numbers and defoliation

canonical.summary: Roots and stems near the soil line appear water-soaked, dark brown and soft, and whole plants or vines collapse quickly; in peppers distinctive black lesions form on rigid stems while foliage and fruit wilt and wither yet remain attached; infected fruit shows water-soaked areas that enlarge and become covered in gray to white sporangia. On eggplant symptoms also include large leaf spots, fruit rot, crown rot, and dieback of the growing tip.
diagnostic_features: In peppers, distinctive black lesions form on stems which remain rigid while foliage and fruit wilt, wither and remain attached; on fruit, sporangia-covered lesions have a yeast-like, gray to white appearance.
treatments: Manage water so that there is never standing water for longer than 24 hours anywhere in the field
Avoid planting susceptible crops in Phytophthora-infested soil and keep records of contaminated fields
Rotate with corn, small grains, brassicas, alliums, or other non-hosts (minimum 3-4 year rotation)
Plant in raised, dome-shaped beds (at least 9 inches for non-vining cucurbits and peppers) in well-drained areas of the field
Practice light irrigation or sub-surface drip irrigation to keep the soil surface dry; improve drainage, break up hardpan with a V-ripper, and avoid soil compaction
After working in infested soil wash soil from equipment, and always work in clean fields before infested fields
Mulch between rows with straw or leave cover crop stubble to reduce splash dispersal of inoculum
Biofumigation with brassica (especially mustard) cover crops
Practice good sanitation and do not discard cull fruit in the field
Avoid introducing the pathogen into a field and promptly destroy affected plants at the start of an outbreak to limit spread
Plant resistant varieties where available (e.g. hard-rinded pumpkins 'Lil' Ironsides', 'Apprentice', 'IronMan', 'Rockafellow', 'CannonBall'; bell peppers 'Conquest', 'Paladin', 'Emerald Isle')
Apply fungicides preventively starting before disease onset
Preventive fungicide programs: mefenoxam/mancozeb (Ridomil, Apron), copper compounds (Kocide, Basic Copper 53, Champ 2F), phosphorous acid fungicides (Prophyt, K-phite, Agri-fos)

Targeted preventive fungicides: in cucurbits Presidio, Ranman, Zing!, Gavel, Zampro, Revus, Curzate, Tanos; for pepper Omega 500 and Reason 500; Presidio, Revus, Forum and phosphorous acid fungicides labeled on eggplant
Soil-applied products: Orondis Gold (in-furrow/banded), Ridomil Gold SL (directed base spray), Regalia Biofungicide, Warhammer (chitosan)
Biofungicides/biologicals: Serenade, Double Nickel, Taegro, RootShield/Rootshield Plus, Actinovate, Mycostop, Stargus, Bexfond, BioTam (soil drench)

canonical.summary: The most characteristic symptoms are root distortion and galling (swelling) that give roots a club-like appearance; aboveground, infected plants are stunted, wilt easily (especially on warm days, often recovering at night) and may show yellowing leaves and blue-green foliage. Clubroot may develop extensively on roots before aboveground symptoms are noticed.
diagnostic_features: Roots are swollen and distorted into large club-shaped malformations ranging from very small swellings on tap and lateral roots to large spindle-shaped clubs; galls are firm with a white interior at the beginning of infection (light-colored early in the season) and eventually turn brown and decay. Clubbing symptoms are unique to members of the Cruciferae.
treatments: Prevent introduction of the pathogen into a field (prevention is the primary control, as the pathogen is long-lived in soil)
Use disease-free, certified transplants; inspect roots for symptoms before planting; reject the entire lot if even a trace of clubroot is present
Sanitize tools and equipment: remove all soil, then apply a surface disinfectant or 1% bleach solution (or a 1:9 household bleach solution / undiluted Lysol), keeping surfaces wet for 15-20 minutes
Only add soil or compost heated to kill pathogens (compost should reach 148 F)
Crop rotation away from susceptible crucifers for a minimum of 4-7 years (Cornell advises at least 7 years; UMN 5-7 years); planting corn or alfalfa can reduce inoculum
Manage weeds and eliminate weedy hosts and brassica crop volunteers during rotation
Raise soil pH by liming to 7.1-7.5 (adjust to ~6.8-7.5 with ground limestone; calcitic lime preferred over dolomitic unless soil magnesium is low; hydrated lime may be added)
Reduce soil moisture: avoid planting in saturated/wet fields, improve drainage, deep-plow, break up hard pan, or use raised beds
Avoid water run-off and irrigation from contaminated fields/ponds into clean areas
Use green manure, organic soil amendments, and soil solarization
Plant clubroot-resistant varieties whenever available
Bury or compost infected plants on site

Fungicides are limited and have not provided adequate or consistent control: e.g., Blocker (PCNB), Omega 500F (fluazinam), Ranman (cyazofamid); see current Cornell/Midwest vegetable production guides for labeled options

canonical.summary: Pythium fruit rot starts as small, water-soaked lesions on fruit near or in contact with the soil; the whole fruit becomes involved within 72 hours, the epidermis ruptures, and the fruit collapses, sometimes with a white, cottony growth on the lesion surface.

treatments: Start with high quality seed grown under optimum temperature, moisture, and nutritional conditions.

Apply fungicides effective against cottony leak: Thrive 4M and Ultra Flourish (mefenoxam) and MetaStar 2E (metalaxyl) - FRAC Group 4 fungicides, applied preplant incorporated or at planting as a soil surface spray.

Deep plow to bury residual inoculum.
Practice a three-year or longer crop rotation with nonhost crops between cucurbit crops.
Use resistant sources: PI 165509, PI 19708-, Marketmore 76.

canonical.summary: On leaves, brown to black circular spots associated with the leaf margins progress toward the center of the leaf; stem and vine cankers form near the nodes with a characteristic brown/reddish gummy exudate and can girdle the plant; on fruit, circular water-soaked spots expand and become black and leathery (black rot).
diagnostic_features: A gummy exudate is usually in the center of diseased spots, which become covered with white mycelium and tiny black fungal fruiting structures (pycnidia, perithecia, and pseudothecia) under high relative humidity; pycnidia swell and release tendrils of spores when wetted.
treatments: Use pathogen-free seed that has been tested for the pathogen, from a reputable company; apply seed treatments if not previously treated
Regularly inspect/scout transplant seedlings in greenhouses and discard seedlings near infected plants; avoid using healthy-looking seedlings from trays with infected plants
Separate cucurbit transplant trays from other vegetables and keep greenhouse humidity below 80% with ventilation
Rotate out of cucurbits for at least 2 years (3-4 years recommended after a confirmed occurrence) using non-host crops such as small grain or corn
Eradicate volunteer cucurbits and wild hosts (wild citrons, balsam pear) before planting
Deep plow / promptly incorporate infected plant debris after harvest to ensure complete decomposition
Avoid overhead irrigation; water in the morning when leaves dry quickly
Apply fungicides preventively and scout routinely for timely application; Chlorothalonil (Bravo) and Mancozeb are effective contact fungicides

Alternate fungicide chemistries / FRAC groups to avoid resistance: carboxamides (Group 7: Endura, Fontelis), DMI (Group 3: Proline, Rhyme), strobilurins (Group 11: Cabrio, Quadris), Topsin M (Group 1), copper (Group M1), Regalia (P5), OSO (Group 19), and premixes (Switch, Pristine, Merivon, Inspire Super, Aprovia Top, Miravis Prime, Orondis Opti, Quadris Top/Opti, ManKocide)
Avoid wounding fruit during harvest; cure winter squash rind (~77Â°F for 1-2 weeks) and store fruit properly (45-50Â°F; ~55Â°F and 60% RH) to prevent postharvest black rot
Biological controls: Double Nickel LC and LifeGard WG
No resistant cucurbit varieties exist (only a very few resistant melon/watermelon varieties)

canonical.summary: Symptoms include wilting, a water-soaked canker with cottony white mycelium at the stem base that turns dark and girdles the plant, middle stalk rot, and head rot leaving a shredded appearance.
diagnostic_features: Sclerotia, formed from the mycelium in shredded tissues, are an excellent method of pathogen identification; a dense, white cottony fungal growth (mycelium) is produced in the stalk.
treatments: Using long rotations with non-host crops such as wheat, corn or sorghum will prevent further build-up in soils
Do not rotate with susceptible crops like dry beans, soybeans, potatoes, or canola
Controlling numerous weed hosts, planting clean seed, burying previous crop debris, and using moderate fertility programs

canonical.summary: Foliar symptoms include chlorotic or necrotic arcs and rings or necrotic line patterns; leaves often have a crisp, leathery texture with curling margins, and plants are stunted with shortened internodes and sidearms.
diagnostic_features: Chlorotic or necrotic arcs and rings or necrotic line patterns; symptoms are suppressed in hot weather and appear during cool weather, so they may occur in leaves of a certain age but not in younger or older leaves.
treatments: Exclusion is an important means of virus control.
Use virus-tested stock certified to be free of viruses.
Clean rootstock is available from the Clean Plant Center Northwest at https://cpcnw.wsu.edu/
Plant where hops have not been grown before or in fields where all hop plants have died out.
General sanitation for disease control.
Work/harvest diseased yards last.
Clean equipment between yards, particularly during early season operations.
Currently, it is recommended that equipment be cleaned by first washing to remove plant debris and then with a 5% to 10% bleach solution for at least a few seconds to upwards of 10 minutes.
Destroy plants that are severely stunted or yellowed.

type_of_disease.quote: ApMV, an ilarvirus previously known in hop as prunus necrotic ringspot virus , can cause up to 30% loss in cone production and also decrease alpha acid levels, but ApMV effects are varietal dependent.

canonical.summary: New shoots can be entirely covered with the fungus and appear white ("flagshoots"); secondary infections on leaves appear as whitish, powdery spots on upper or lower leaf surfaces, sometimes preceded by a small blister. Infected cones are stunted, malformed, and mature rapidly, and infected areas on cones become red to blackish if chasmothecia are produced.
diagnostic_features: White, circular powdery colonies on leaves; entire white shoots (flagshoots) typical in spring; infected cones are stunted, malformed, and mature rapidly, leading to cone shatter, with infected areas becoming red to blackish if chasmothecia are produced.
treatments: Reduce or eliminate infected buds and flag shoots by crowning, harrowing, burning, etc. Treating before shoots emerge reduces early-season spread within a field.
Completely removing green tissue during preparation for training reduces spore load and subsequent secondary spread.
Maintain adequate nitrogen levels but do not over-apply because more succulent tissue is more susceptible.
Scout yards regularly for signs of powdery mildew.
Control bottom growth after training, mechanically or with burn-back herbicides, etc., in order to reduce active colonies.
Strip lower leaves up to about 4 ft in order to break the "green bridge" that facilitates powdery mildew's climb up in the canopy.
Early harvest can reduce powdery mildew losses in fields with high disease pressure.
Remove seedlings from around harvesting shed and hop dryer. Remove pole plants. Eliminate feral hops.
Protect regrowth against infection or remove shoot regrowth (mow, desiccate, flail, flame, etc.).
Replace highly susceptible varieties.
Thorough spray coverage is essential to protect hop plants; spray every row. Apply protective fungicides before disease is reproducing and spreading.
Bicarbonates are registered to control powdery mildew (Bi-Carb Old Fashioned Fungicide, HO Carb-O-Nator, Kaligreen, MilStop SP, Vacres).

Demethylation-inhibiting (DMI) Fungicides (Group 3) are labeled for use. Alternate or tank-mix with a non-Group 3 fungicide for resistance management (Procure 480SC, Rally 40WSP, Rhyme, Sonoma 40WSP, Tebustar 3.6L, Tebuzol 3.6F, Topguard).
Luna Experience (Group 7 + 3), Luna Sensation (Group 7 + 11), Magister SC (Group 39).
Oils are labeled to control hop powdery mildew (IAP Organic 440 Spray Oil, JMS Stylet Oil, 440 Superior Spray Oil, Trilogy).
Quintec (Group 13).
Regalia Biofungicide (Group P5).
Strobilurin fungicides (Group 11) are labeled for use (Flint Extra, Pristine).
Sulfur formulations are registered for hop (Microthiol Disperss, Proganic Micronized Sulfur); primarily a protectant and must be applied before infection.
Torino (Group U6).
Biological control (Actinovate AG, Double Nickel LC, Ecoswing, Romeo, Sonata) â€” efficacy unknown in the Pacific Northwest.
